fuentes/sermon-de-montesinos/titulo.texto: Advent Sermon of Antonio de Montesinos

fuentes/sermon-de-montesinos/soporte.texto: Oral sermon; the text is known through Las Casas’s Historia de las Indias

fuentes/sermon-de-montesinos/resumen.texto: Sermon preached in December 1511 in Santo Domingo by the Dominican Antonio de Montesinos, on behalf of his community, before the authorities and the encomenderos of Hispaniola. He asked by what right the Indigenous people were subjected to servitude and war (“Are these not men?”) and announced that the friars would not absolve those who kept them that way. No text written by Montesinos survives; the known version is the one Las Casas included decades later in his Historia de las Indias.

fuentes/sermon-de-montesinos/por_que_imp.texto: It is the first documented public protest against the treatment of Indigenous people in the Americas. The settlers’ complaint to the king led to the junta that drafted the Laws of Burgos.

fuentes/sermon-de-montesinos/leer.0.titu.texto: Las Casas’s Historia de las Indias, vol. 3, with the account of the sermons (book III, chapters 3 to 5), at Project Gutenberg

fuentes/leyes-de-burgos/titulo.texto: Laws of Burgos (Ordinances for the Good Order and Treatment of the Indians)

fuentes/leyes-de-burgos/resumen.texto: Thirty-five ordinances signed by Ferdinand the Catholic in Burgos on December 27, 1512, after the junta convened in response to the Dominicans’ protests. They accepted the encomienda and the forced labor of Indigenous people, but regulated it: work and rest periods, food, limits on punishments, exclusion of pregnant women from mine labor, and the obligation to teach the doctrine. An addition of 1513, signed in Valladolid, limited the labor of women and children.

fuentes/leyes-de-burgos/por_que_importa.texto: It is the Crown’s first general legislation for the Indigenous people of the Americas. It was poorly enforced, and the population decline in the Caribbean continued.

fuentes/requerimiento/resumen.texto: Text drafted around 1513 by the jurist Juan López de Palacios Rubios, which captains were to read to Indigenous people before waging war on them. It explained the creation of the world, the authority of the pope and the donation of the Indies to the kings of Castile, and demanded that the listeners accept that authority and the preaching. If they did not, the war, slavery and the loss of their goods would be their own fault. It was read in Castilian, often without an interpreter.

fuentes/requerimiento/por_que_importa.texto: It shows the legal reasoning with which the Crown justified the war of conquest. Defenders of Indigenous people criticized it as a legal fiction, and the Ordinances of 1573 replaced it with a procedure of “pacification.”

fuentes/inter-caetera/resumen.texto: Bull of Pope Alexander VI granting the Catholic Monarchs and their successors the islands and mainland lands discovered or to be discovered west of a line drawn pole to pole one hundred leagues west of the Azores and Cape Verde, with the obligation to send missionaries to convert their inhabitants. It forms part of the so-called Alexandrine bulls, issued in 1493 at the Crown’s request after Columbus’s first voyage.

fuentes/inter-caetera/por_que_importa.texto: It was the main legal title invoked by Castile for its dominion in the Americas. Vitoria later debated whether the pope had the power to grant those lands, and Portugal negotiated moving the line at Tordesillas.

fuentes/tratado-de-tordesillas/autor.texto: Catholic Monarchs and John II of Portugal

fuentes/tratado-de-tordesillas/resumen.texto: Treaty signed on June 7, 1494, between the Catholic Monarchs and John II of Portugal, which divided the lands yet to be discovered with a meridian located 370 leagues west of the Cape Verde islands: the west for Castile and the east for Portugal. It shifted westward the line set by the bull Inter caetera.

fuentes/tratado-de-tordesillas/por_que_i.texto: It explains why Brazil fell to Portugal. It was the basis of boundary disputes in the River Plate basin, such as the one over the Colonia del Sacramento, until the Treaty of Madrid of 1750 replaced it.

fuentes/tratado-de-tordesillas/leer.0.ti.texto: English translation at the Avalon Project (Yale University)

fuentes/testamento-de-isabel-la-catolica.texto: Will and Codicil of Isabella the Catholic

Will signed by Queen Isabella in Medina del Campo on October 12, 1504, with a codicil dated November 23, three days before her death. In the codicil she asks her successors not to allow the Indigenous people of the islands and mainland to be wronged in their persons or property, and to have them treated well and justly.
It was cited for centuries as proof of the Crown’s protective intent. Its critics recall that a royal decree of 1503 had already authorized compelling Indigenous people to work for the settlers.

fuentes/sublimis-deus/resumen.texto: Papal bull of Paul III, issued in 1537, that declared the Indigenous people of the Americas to be true men, capable of receiving the faith, and said they must not be deprived of their liberty or property even if they were not Christians. It responded to reports from Dominican friars working in Mexico.

fuentes/sublimis-deus/por_que_importa.texto: It was the most cited papal position in defense of Indigenous people. Charles V objected that papal documents on the Indies circulated without his authorization, and in 1538 the pope revoked the brief that imposed penalties on those who enslaved them.

fuentes/relectio-de-indis/titulo.texto: Relectiones on the Indians and on the Law of War

fuentes/relectio-de-indis/soporte.texto: Public lectures at the University of Salamanca; printed in Lyon in 1557

fuentes/relectio-de-indis/resumen.texto: Two lectures by Francisco de Vitoria at Salamanca on the titles that could justify Spanish dominion in the Americas. He held that Indigenous people were the true owners of their lands and goods, and he rejected as titles the universal lordship of the emperor or the pope, the right of discovery, and the sins of the Indigenous people. He accepted instead others, such as the right of communication and commerce among peoples, the freedom to preach, and the defense of the innocent, which could justify war if they were violated.

fuentes/relectio-de-indis/por_que_import.texto: It is the founding text of the School of Salamanca and is regarded as an antecedent of international law. Its critics point out that the titles it admitted left open the justification of conquest.

fuentes/relectio-de-indis/leer.0.titulo.texto: 1557 Lyon edition of the lectures (Internet Archive)

fuentes/democrates-alter/titulo.texto: Democrates Alter, or On the Just Causes of War against the Indians

fuentes/democrates-alter/soporte.texto: Manuscript; the universities of Salamanca and Alcalá advised against printing it, and it was published only in 1892

fuentes/democrates-alter/resumen.texto: Dialogue in Latin in which Sepúlveda defends the lawfulness of war against the Indigenous peoples of the Americas. His arguments are Aristotle’s natural servitude, applied to peoples he judged barbarians; the duty to stop practices such as human sacrifice and cannibalism; the protection of innocent victims; and the need to ensure preaching.

fuentes/democrates-alter/por_que_importa.texto: It is the most systematic exposition of the position favoring conquest by arms. It was the basis of Sepúlveda’s defense against Las Casas at the Valladolid junta.

fuentes/leyes-nuevas/resumen.texto: Ordinances signed by Charles V in Barcelona on November 20, 1542, and expanded in Valladolid in 1543. They prohibited enslaving Indigenous people for any cause, ruled that encomiendas could not be inherited and would end with their holders, removed those held by officials and religious institutions, and created the Viceroyalty of Peru and the Audiencia of Lima.

fuentes/leyes-nuevas/por_que_importa.texto: They provoked the rebellion of the encomenderos of Peru led by Gonzalo Pizarro. In 1545 the Crown revoked the clause that abolished the inheritance of encomiendas. Even so, they mark the high point of the reform promoted by Las Casas and his allies.

fuentes/capitulacion-de-pedro-de-mendoza.texto: Contract signed in Toledo on May 21, 1534, between Charles V and Pedro de Mendoza to conquer and settle the Río de la Plata. It named him adelantado and governor of a strip two hundred leagues south of the governorships granted in Peru, required him to bring one thousand men at his own expense and to build fortresses, and promised him titles and a share of the treasures obtained.
It shows how the Crown delegated conquest to private individuals in exchange for titles and profits. The first founding of Buenos Aires came out of it.

fuentes/carta-de-luis-ramirez/titulo.texto: Letter of Luis Ramírez from the Río de la Plata

fuentes/carta-de-luis-ramirez/resumen.texto: Letter written on July 10, 1528, by Luis Ramírez, a crew member of Sebastian Cabot’s expedition, to his father, from the port of San Salvador on the Uruguay River. It recounts the voyage, the founding of Fort Sancti Spíritus, the exploration of the Paraná, the hunger, and the reports of a range rich in silver that attracted the expedition.

fuentes/carta-de-luis-ramirez/por_que_im.texto: It is considered the first written text from the Río de la Plata region. It is a direct source on the Cabot expedition and the peoples of the Paraná.

fuentes/carta-de-isabel-de-guevara/titul.texto: Letter from Isabel de Guevara to Princess Juana

fuentes/carta-de-isabel-de-guevara/resum.texto: Letter dated in Asunción on July 2, 1556, and addressed to the princess governor Joanna of Austria. It describes the hunger of the first Buenos Aires, when, according to the author, the women washed clothes, nursed the sick, stood guard and rowed because the men were weak. It asks for a repartimiento of Indigenous people for herself and her husband.

fuentes/carta-de-isabel-de-guevara/por_q.texto: It is one of the few written testimonies by a woman about the conquest of the Río de la Plata, and a source on the unequal distribution of encomiendas among the first settlers.

fuentes/carta-de-isabel-de-guevara/leer..texto: Cartas de Indias (Madrid, 1877), which publishes the letter (Internet Archive)

fuentes/ordenanzas-de-poblacion-1573/tit.texto: Ordinances on Discovery, New Settlement and Pacification of the Indies

fuentes/ordenanzas-de-poblacion-1573/sop.texto: Signed in the forest of Segovia on July 13, 1573

fuentes/ordenanzas-de-poblacion-1573/res.texto: One hundred and forty-eight ordinances by Philip II that regulated new discoveries and the founding of cities. They set the grid layout around a main plaza, the choice of site, the allotment of building lots, and the formation of the cabildo. They replaced the word “conquest” with “pacification,” with instructions to attract Indigenous people by peaceful means.

fuentes/ordenanzas-de-poblacion-1573/por.texto: They gave regulatory form to the cities founded after 1573, such as Salta, Corrientes, La Rioja, Jujuy and the second Buenos Aires. Their critics point out that the change of wording did not prevent the wars that followed.

fuentes/ordenanzas-de-alfaro/resumen.texto: Ordinances issued by the oidor Francisco de Alfaro during his visit to Paraguay, the Río de la Plata and Tucumán. They prohibited personal service and the enslavement of Indigenous people, set a tribute in money or in kind, allowed wage labor for a limited time, regulated the mita and protected the pueblos de indios. The encomenderos resisted them, and the Council of the Indies confirmed them with modifications in 1618.

fuentes/ordenanzas-de-alfaro/por_que_imp.texto: They were the main attempt to apply protective legislation in the region. The Jesuit reductions, whose Indigenous people stood outside the encomiendas, drew on them. Their enforcement was partial.

fuentes/politica-indiana/resumen.texto: Expanded Castilian version of De Indiarum iure (1629–1639), in which Solórzano sets out the law of the Indies: the titles to Spanish dominion, the condition of Indigenous people, the encomienda, the mita and personal service, civil and ecclesiastical government, and the Royal Treasury. He defends the legitimacy of the conquest and of the Crown’s dominion and, at the same time, the legal protection of Indigenous people as “wretched” persons who needed shelter.

fuentes/politica-indiana/por_que_importa.texto: It was the reference work of jurists and officials for more than a century, and it was reprinted several times in the 18th century. It is the classic exposition of Indian law written from within the system.

fuentes/recopilacion-de-indias-1680/titu.texto: Compilation of the Laws of the Kingdoms of the Indies

fuentes/recopilacion-de-indias-1680/auto.texto: Council of the Indies, by order of Charles II

fuentes/recopilacion-de-indias-1680/sopo.texto: Four volumes printed in Madrid in 1681

fuentes/recopilacion-de-indias-1680/resu.texto: Official compilation of the law issued for America, promulgated by Charles II in 1680 and based on the work of Antonio de León Pinelo and Juan de Solórzano. In nine books it arranges thousands of laws on the Church, the audiencias, viceroys, commerce, the Royal Treasury and Indigenous people, including the rules on the encomienda, the mita and personal service.

fuentes/recopilacion-de-indias-1680/por_.texto: It was the body of law in force in the Río de la Plata for the rest of the colonial period, and it continued to apply in part after independence. The gap between its protective norms and their enforcement is one of the axes of the debate over the Black Legend.

fuentes/tratado-de-lisboa-1681/autor.texto: Charles II of Spain and Peter II of Portugal

fuentes/tratado-de-lisboa-1681/resumen.texto: Treaty of May 7, 1681, by which Spain disapproved the assault by Governor José de Garro on the Colonia del Sacramento. Spain agreed to remove him from his post and to return the post to Portugal with its artillery, while a commission and, if it did not agree, the pope would decide to whom the territory belonged.

fuentes/tratado-de-lisboa-1681/por_que_i.texto: It established the Portuguese presence facing Buenos Aires, which would last, with interruptions, until 1777.

fuentes/tratado-del-asiento-1713/titulo.texto: Asiento de Negros with Great Britain

fuentes/tratado-del-asiento-1713/autor.texto: Crowns of Spain and Great Britain

fuentes/tratado-del-asiento-1713/resumen.texto: Contract signed on March 26, 1713, and incorporated into the Peace of Utrecht, by which the Spanish Crown granted Great Britain, for thirty years, the monopoly on selling African slaves in its colonies, at a rate of 4,800 “piezas de Indias” a year. Great Britain ceded it to the South Sea Company. The contract allowed slaves to be introduced through Buenos Aires and an annual ship of merchandise to be sent to the American fairs.

fuentes/tratado-del-asiento-1713/por_que.texto: It made Buenos Aires one of the legal ports of entry for slaves into the Viceroyalty of Peru, and it opened a route that was also used for British smuggling.

fuentes/tratado-de-madrid-1750/autor.texto: Ferdinand VI of Spain and John V of Portugal

fuentes/tratado-de-madrid-1750/resumen.texto: Boundary treaty signed on January 13, 1750, that replaced the Tordesillas line with borders based on effective possession. Portugal handed the Colonia del Sacramento to Spain, and Spain ceded to Portugal the seven missionary towns of the Guaraní east of the Uruguay River, whose inhabitants were to move with their movable goods.

fuentes/tratado-de-madrid-1750/por_que_i.texto: The order to abandon the seven towns provoked the Guaraní War (1754–1756). The treaty was annulled in 1761, and the Jesuits’ enemies blamed them for the resistance, one of the antecedents of their expulsion.

fuentes/tratado-de-el-pardo-1761/autor.texto: Charles III of Spain and Joseph I of Portugal

fuentes/tratado-de-el-pardo-1761/resumen.texto: Treaty of February 12, 1761, that annulled the Treaty of Madrid of 1750 and restored the earlier situation: the Colonia del Sacramento remained Portuguese, and the seven missionary towns were Spanish.

fuentes/tratado-de-el-pardo-1761/por_que.texto: It closed, without result, the exchange that had led to the Guaraní War, and it left open the dispute over the Colonia, which Pedro de Cevallos took the following year.

fuentes/pragmatica-de-expulsion-1767/tit.texto: Pragmatic Sanction on the Expulsion of the Jesuits

fuentes/pragmatica-de-expulsion-1767/res.texto: Pragmatic sanction of April 2, 1767, by which Charles III, based on a decree of February 27, expelled the Society of Jesus from all his dominions and seized its goods. It gave no public reasons: the king said he reserved them in his royal mind, although the investigation that prepared it blamed the Jesuits for the Esquilache Riot of 1766.

fuentes/pragmatica-de-expulsion-1767/por.texto: In the Río de la Plata it ended the Jesuit administration of the Guaraní missions, passed the University of Córdoba to the Franciscans, and led to the sale of the estancias by the Junta de Temporalidades. Its causes are debated among the regalism of the Bourbon monarchy, the conflict over the missions and the economic power of the order.

fuentes/naufragios-y-comentarios/soporte.texto: Book printed in Valladolid in 1555; the Relación had already been published in Zamora in 1542

fuentes/naufragios-y-comentarios/resumen.texto: Joint edition of two accounts. The Relación, known as Naufragios, narrates the failure of Narváez’s expedition in Florida (1527) and the eight years that Álvar Núñez and three companions spent among Indigenous peoples until reaching Mexico. The Comentarios, written by his secretary Pero Hernández, describe his government of the Río de la Plata: the overland journey from the Brazilian coast to Asunción, the exploration of the upper Paraguay, and his deposition in 1544.

fuentes/naufragios-y-comentarios/por_que.texto: The Comentarios are Álvar Núñez’s case against Irala and the royal officials who deposed him. They should be read together with contrary accounts, such as Schmidl’s.

fuentes/naufragios-y-comentarios/leer.2..texto: The Comentarios in English, with Schmidl’s voyage (The Conquest of the River Plate, Hakluyt Society, 1891)

fuentes/la-argentina-ruy-diaz/titulo.texto: La Argentina (Annals of the Discovery, Settlement and Conquest of the Provinces of the Río de la Plata)

fuentes/la-argentina-ruy-diaz/soporte.texto: Manuscript; first published by Pedro de Angelis in 1835

fuentes/la-argentina-ruy-diaz/resumen.texto: History of the conquest of the Río de la Plata and Paraguay from Solís to the late 16th century, completed in La Plata de los Charcas in 1612 by a mestizo grandson of Irala. It combines oral testimonies of conquistadors with legendary accounts, such as that of Lucía Miranda, and defends Irala’s family.

fuentes/la-argentina-ruy-diaz/por_que_im.texto: It is the first history of the region written by someone born there, and it helped spread the name “Argentina.” Its data must be checked against documents, because he wrote decades after the events.

fuentes/la-argentina-centenera/titulo.texto: Argentina and the Conquest of the Río de la Plata

fuentes/la-argentina-centenera/soporte.texto: Poem in twenty-eight cantos printed in Lisbon in 1602

fuentes/la-argentina-centenera/resumen.texto: Epic poem in ottava rima on the conquest of the Río de la Plata, Paraguay, Tucumán and Peru, which the author traveled through from 1573. It narrates the expeditions, the struggles with Indigenous peoples, the nature of the region and episodes from Peru in his time, in a moralizing tone.

fuentes/la-argentina-centenera/por_que_i.texto: It is the first printed book to call the Río de la Plata region “Argentina,” from the Latin argentum, silver. Its historical value is uneven, but it is direct testimony of the Ortiz de Zárate expedition.

fuentes/conquista-espiritual/titulo.texto: Spiritual Conquest carried out by the religious of the Society of Jesus in the provinces of Paraguay, Paraná, Uruguay and Tape

fuentes/conquista-espiritual/resumen.texto: Account of the founding of the Guaraní reductions of Guairá, Paraná, Uruguay and Tape, written by one of its missionaries for the court in Madrid. It describes Guaraní life and the organization of the villages and, in detail, the attacks by the bandeirantes of São Paulo, who captured Indigenous people to sell them as slaves, and the exodus of 1631 and 1632.

fuentes/conquista-espiritual/por_que_imp.texto: It was the case the Jesuits made to win the Crown’s support against the bandeirantes. It is a central source, though written to defend the order.

fuentes/tesoro-de-la-lengua-guarani/resu.texto: Guaraní-Castilian dictionary by Ruiz de Montoya, with thousands of entries and phrases in use, published in 1639. The following year his Arte y bocabulario de la lengua guaraní came out, with the grammar and the Castilian-Guaraní dictionary. It records the Guaraní spoken in the reductions in the first decades of the 17th century.

fuentes/tesoro-de-la-lengua-guarani/por_.texto: It is the basis for the study of Old Guaraní and evidence of the Jesuit policy of evangelizing in an Indigenous language.

fuentes/historia-provinciae-paraquariae/.texto: History of the Province of Paraguay of the Society of Jesus

History in Latin of the Jesuit province of Paraguay from the arrival of the first Jesuits in Tucumán to the mid-17th century, written by the French Jesuit Nicolas du Toict, known in Spanish as Nicolás del Techo, who was a missionary in the region. It narrates the founding of colleges and reductions, the missions to the Chaco and the attacks by the bandeirantes.
It is one of the first general histories of the Jesuit province and spread among European readers the image of the reductions.

fuentes/historia-de-la-conquista-lozano/.texto: History of the Conquest of Paraguay, Río de la Plata and Tucumán
Manuscript; published by Andrés Lamas in Buenos Aires between 1873 and 1875

General history of the conquest of the region, written by the official chronicler of the Jesuits, with access to the order’s archives and to documents from the cabildos. It covers the expeditions, the foundations, the wars with Indigenous peoples and the government of the cities up to the mid-18th century.
It is one of the most complete sources for the period, written from the point of view of the Society of Jesus.

fuentes/descripcion-del-gran-chaco/titul.texto: Chorographic Description of the Gran Chaco Gualamba

fuentes/descripcion-del-gran-chaco/resum.texto: Description of the territory, rivers, flora, fauna and peoples of the Gran Chaco, with the history of the Spanish expeditions and of the missions in the region. Lozano compiled it from reports by missionaries and military expeditions.

fuentes/descripcion-del-gran-chaco/por_q.texto: It is the first comprehensive work on the Chaco and a main source on its Indigenous peoples in the 18th century, seen from the missionary perspective.

fuentes/histoire-du-paraguay/resumen.texto: History of the conquest of the Río de la Plata and Paraguay and, above all, of the Jesuit missions, written in France with the order’s documents by a Jesuit who had never known the region. It includes documentary appendices and defends the Society against accusations about the reductions.

fuentes/histoire-du-paraguay/por_que_imp.texto: It was published at the height of the European controversy against the Jesuits, when their enemies presented the Guaraní War as proof of a “Jesuit kingdom.” It is a piece of that dispute and a source of documents.

fuentes/cristianesimo-felice/titulo.texto: Happy Christianity in the Missions of the Fathers of the Society of Jesus in Paraguay

fuentes/cristianesimo-felice/resumen.texto: Laudatory description of the Guaraní reductions as an exemplary Christian community, with work and goods held largely in common, without money and under the paternal government of the missionaries. Muratori wrote it in Italy from letters and reports by Jesuits, without knowing the region.

fuentes/cristianesimo-felice/por_que_imp.texto: It was one of the texts that created the image of the missions as a utopia, later taken up by the “rosy legend.” The Enlightenment enemies of the Jesuits held the opposite image of a despotic power.

fuentes/candido-voltaire/resumen.texto: Satirical novel against philosophical optimism, in which the protagonist travels through Europe and America. In the chapters on Paraguay, Voltaire presents the government of the Jesuits as a kingdom in which “the fathers have everything and the peoples nothing,” at the height of the European campaign against the Society after the Guaraní War.

fuentes/candido-voltaire/por_que_importa.texto: It shows how the French Enlightenment built the opposite image to the idealization of the missions. It is literature, not testimony.

fuentes/historia-de-abiponibus/soporte.texto: Three volumes; there was a contemporary German translation and an English one in 1822

fuentes/historia-de-abiponibus/resumen.texto: Work in three volumes in which Dobrizhoffer, a missionary for about eighteen years, describes the Abipones, an equestrian people of the Chaco: their language, customs, wars and beliefs, and their life in the reductions. It also covers the nature of the region and news about the Guaraníes and the Spaniards of Paraguay.

fuentes/historia-de-abiponibus/por_que_i.texto: It is one of the richest ethnographic sources on the peoples of the Chaco in the 18th century, written in exile and from a missionary’s point of view.

fuentes/historia-de-abiponibus/leer.0.ti.texto: Latin edition of Vienna of 1784 (Internet Archive)

fuentes/historia-de-abiponibus/leer.1.ti.texto: English translation of 1822, volume 1, on Project Gutenberg

fuentes/hacia-alla-y-para-aca/titulo.texto: Hacia allá y para acá (A Stay Among the Mocobí Indians)

fuentes/hacia-alla-y-para-aca/soporte.texto: Manuscript illustrated with watercolors, kept at the Zwettl monastery; translated into Spanish and published in Tucumán between 1942 and 1944

fuentes/hacia-alla-y-para-aca/resumen.texto: Chronicle of a Jesuit missionary among the Mocoví people of the San Javier reduction, north of Santa Fe, written after the expulsion. It recounts the journey, the founding and life of the reduction, cattle raising, trades, music and Mocoví customs, illustrated with the author’s watercolors.

fuentes/hacia-alla-y-para-aca/por_que_im.texto: Its illustrations are one of the most important visual records of life in the Litoral and the Chaco in the 18th century.

fuentes/de-administratione-guaranica/tit.texto: Commentary on Guaraní Administration Compared with Plato’s Republic

fuentes/de-administratione-guaranica/res.texto: Work by a Catalan Jesuit who had taught in Córdoba, written in Italian exile, which compares point by point the organization of the Guaraní reductions with Plato’s ideal republic. It highlights the combination of common lands and goods (tupambaé) with the family plot (abambaé), organized labor and the absence of luxury.

fuentes/de-administratione-guaranica/por.texto: It is the most elaborate version of the idea of the missions as an ideal republic, written by an expelled Jesuit who defended his order.

fuentes/diferencia-entre-lo-temporal-y-l.texto: On the Difference Between the Temporal and the Eternal (mission edition)
Juan Eusebio Nieremberg; Guaraní translation by José Serrano
Book printed on the mission press, with engravings made in the reductions

Guaraní translation of the devotional treatise by the Spanish Jesuit Juan Eusebio Nieremberg, printed in 1705 in the missions with type cast there and illustrated with engravings made by Guaraní craftsmen.
It is one of the first printed books in the Plata basin and shows the technical and artistic production of the reductions.

fuentes/doctrina-christiana-1584/titulo.texto: Christian Doctrine and Catechism for the Instruction of the Indians

fuentes/doctrina-christiana-1584/soporte.texto: Printed in Lima by Antonio Ricardo

fuentes/doctrina-christiana-1584/resumen.texto: Trilingual catechism approved by the Third Council of Lima (1582–1583) and published in 1584. It was the first book printed in South America and fixed the doctrinal texts to be taught in Quechua and Aymara throughout the Viceroyalty of Peru, including Tucumán.

fuentes/doctrina-christiana-1584/por_que.texto: It marks the Church’s decision in the viceroyalty to evangelize in the general Indigenous languages, as the bishops of Tucumán and Paraguay also did with Quechua and Guaraní.

fuentes/lazarillo-de-ciegos-caminantes/t.texto: The Lazarillo of Blind Travelers from Buenos Aires to Lima

fuentes/lazarillo-de-ciegos-caminantes/s.texto: Printed in Lima around 1775 with a false imprint (“Gijón, 1773”)

fuentes/lazarillo-de-ciegos-caminantes/r.texto: Account of the postal inspection journey of Carrió de la Vandera between Buenos Aires and Lima (1771–1773), signed with the name of his companion from Cuzco, Calixto Bustamante Carlos Inca, alias Concolorcorvo, who was taken as the author until the 20th century. It describes the post stations, distances and costs of the road, the cities of Córdoba, Tucumán, Salta and Jujuy, the mule trade, the life of the gauderios in the countryside and conflicts with Indigenous peoples.

fuentes/lazarillo-de-ciegos-caminantes/p.texto: It is one of the liveliest sources on the route from the Río de la Plata to Peru at the end of the colonial period, and it contains one of the first descriptions of the forerunners of the gaucho.

fuentes/relacion-de-acarete/titulo.texto: Account of the Voyages of Acarete du Biscay to the Río de la Plata and Overland to Peru

fuentes/relacion-de-acarete/soporte.texto: Published in the travel collection of Melchisédech Thévenot

fuentes/relacion-de-acarete/resumen.texto: Account by a French traveler who arrived in Buenos Aires around 1658 and continued overland to Potosí. It describes Buenos Aires and its trade in hides and silver, Córdoba, Santiago del Estero, Salta and Potosí, and the circulation of goods and slaves outside the prohibitions.

fuentes/relacion-de-acarete/por_que_impo.texto: It is one of the few foreign testimonies on the Río de la Plata in the 17th century and a source on the illegal trade through Buenos Aires.

fuentes/el-imperio-jesuitico/resumen.texto: Historical essay that Leopoldo Lugones wrote at the request of the Argentine government after touring the ruins of Misiones. It describes the conquest, the founding of the reductions, their architecture and organization, and judges the Jesuit regime a theocracy that kept the Guaraníes under tutelage.

fuentes/el-imperio-jesuitico/por_que_imp.texto: It shows the liberal and positivist Argentine view of the missions at the beginning of the 20th century, opposed to the Catholic idealization, and it helped spread the ruins as heritage.

fuentes/a-vanished-arcadia/resumen.texto: Account by the Scottish writer Robert Bontine Cunninghame Graham, who had lived in the Río de la Plata, of the Jesuit missions of Paraguay from 1607 to the expulsion. It presents the reductions sympathetically, as a simple society protected from the settlers, and laments their destruction.

fuentes/a-vanished-arcadia/por_que_impor.texto: It spread the romantic image of the missions in the English-speaking world.

fuentes/brevisima-relacion/titulo.texto: A Short Account of the Destruction of the Indies

fuentes/brevisima-relacion/soporte.texto: Written in 1542 for Prince Philip; printed in Seville in 1552

fuentes/brevisima-relacion/resumen.texto: Report by Las Casas that goes region by region through the massacres, enslavements and abuses of the conquistadors, to persuade the Crown to abolish the encomiendas and the conquests. It was written in 1542, when the New Laws were being prepared, and published in 1552. Its death toll of more than twelve million, and according to the author probably more than fifteen, does not come from a count, and historians consider it exaggerated, although the decline of the Indigenous population he describes is documented by other sources.

fuentes/brevisima-relacion/por_que_impor.texto: It was translated into Dutch, French, English, Latin and German between 1578 and 1599 and, with the engravings of Theodor de Bry, became the central piece of propaganda against Spain. For some it is the text that founds the black legend; for others, an exaggerated but essentially truthful testimony.

fuentes/brevisima-relacion/leer.2.titulo.texto: Latin edition of 1598 with De Bry’s engravings (Internet Archive)

fuentes/apologia-de-orange/titulo.texto: Apology of the Prince of Orange

fuentes/apologia-de-orange/autor.texto: William of Orange, drafted by Pierre Loyseleur de Villiers

fuentes/apologia-de-orange/resumen.texto: Response by William of Orange, presented to the States General at the end of 1580 and published in 1581, to the edict by which Philip II had outlawed him. It accuses the king of private and public crimes and invokes the cruelties of the Spaniards in America as proof of his tyranny.

fuentes/apologia-de-orange/por_que_impor.texto: It is one of the foundational pieces of the anti-Spanish propaganda of the Dutch war, which joined the denunciations about America with the accusations against Philip II and the Inquisition.

fuentes/americae-de-bry/soporte.texto: Thirteen parts with copper engravings, continued by De Bry’s sons

fuentes/americae-de-bry/resumen.texto: Collection of accounts of voyages to America published in Frankfurt, with hundreds of engravings based on drawings and texts by travelers: Thomas Harriot and John White in Virginia, Hans Staden in Brazil and Girolamo Benzoni on the Spanish conquest, among others. Its images of cannibalism, martyrdom and Spanish cruelties were reproduced for centuries.

fuentes/americae-de-bry/por_que_importa.texto: Together with the illustrated edition of the Brevísima (1598), it gave visual form to the black legend in Protestant Europe. The images are the work of engravers who never set foot in America.

fuentes/americae-de-bry/leer.0.titulo.texto: Americae pars sexta (1596), with Benzoni’s history (Internet Archive)

fuentes/tears-of-the-indians/soporte.texto: Translation by John Phillips, dedicated to Oliver Cromwell

fuentes/tears-of-the-indians/resumen.texto: English translation of the Brevísima relación made by John Phillips, nephew of John Milton, and dedicated to Oliver Cromwell in 1656, when England was at war with Spain after launching its expedition against the Spanish Antilles.

fuentes/tears-of-the-indians/por_que_imp.texto: It shows the political use of Las Casas’s work in English propaganda, which presented the war against Spain as punishment for its crimes in America.

fuentes/la-leyenda-negra-juderias/titulo.texto: The Black Legend and Historical Truth

fuentes/la-leyenda-negra-juderias/resume.texto: Essay awarded by the magazine La Ilustración Española y Americana that gathers foreign criticisms of Spain, from the Inquisition and the conquest of America to economic backwardness. It argues that they form a legend built by its Protestant rivals and by the Enlightenment, and compares the accusations against Spain with the abuses of other colonial powers.

fuentes/la-leyenda-negra-juderias/por_qu.texto: It spread the expression “black legend” and set the comparative argument of the defense of Spain. Its critics point out that, in denouncing propaganda, it tended to minimize documented facts.

fuentes/historia-de-la-leyenda-negra-car.texto: History of the Hispano-American Black Legend

Study by the Argentine historian Rómulo Carbia on the origin and spread of the black legend, with a critical analysis of the works of Las Casas, whom he accuses of exaggerating and distorting the facts, and of their use by Protestant propaganda and the Enlightenment.
It is the main Argentine work of Catholic Hispanism on the subject. Its critics object to its hostility toward Las Casas and its tendency to dismiss as propaganda testimonies that are documented.

fuentes/spanish-struggle-for-justice/tit.texto: The Spanish Struggle for Justice in the Conquest of America

fuentes/spanish-struggle-for-justice/res.texto: Study of the debates that accompanied the conquest: Montesinos’s sermon, the Laws of Burgos, the Requerimiento, the New Laws, the Valladolid junta and the experiments in peaceful colonization. It argues that no other colonial power discussed the justice of its conquest so seriously.

fuentes/spanish-struggle-for-justice/por.texto: It offered an academic reading distinct both from the black legend and from apologetics. Benjamin Keen objected in 1969 that it exaggerated the influence of those debates on colonial practice.

fuentes/black-legend-revisited/titulo.texto: The Black Legend Revisited: Assumptions and Realities

fuentes/black-legend-revisited/soporte.texto: Article in the Hispanic American Historical Review

fuentes/black-legend-revisited/resumen.texto: Article in which Benjamin Keen discusses the interpretation of Lewis Hanke and of the historians who relativized the black legend. He argues that the protective legislation had little application and that the exploitation of Indigenous labor and the population decline were structural features of the colonial regime, not exceptions.

fuentes/black-legend-revisited/por_que_i.texto: It opened, with Hanke, a debate in the same journal that sums up the two academic readings of the conquest: the weight of the laws and debates, or that of economic practices.

fuentes/modest-proposal-hanke/titulo.texto: A Modest Proposal for a Moratorium on Grand Generalizations

fuentes/modest-proposal-hanke/soporte.texto: Article in the Hispanic American Historical Review

fuentes/modest-proposal-hanke/resumen.texto: Lewis Hanke’s reply to Benjamin Keen, in which he proposes setting aside generalizations about Spanish cruelty or benevolence and studying specific regions, periods and institutions before judging the conquest as a whole.

fuentes/modest-proposal-hanke/por_que_im.texto: Keen answered him that same year in the same journal. The proposal to study specific cases coincides with the path later historiography followed.

fuentes/tree-of-hate/resumen.texto: Essay that traces hispanophobia from Protestant propaganda of the 16th century to the culture and politics of the United States in the 20th century. It argues that the black legend was transmitted through school textbooks, English-language historiography and foreign policy toward Latin America.

fuentes/tree-of-hate/por_que_importa.texto: It is the reference work for those who see the black legend as a prejudice still in force. Its critics consider it polemical and not attentive to the facts that the propaganda exaggerated but did not invent.

fuentes/las-indias-no-eran-colonias/resu.texto: Essay in which Ricardo Levene argues that, under the law of the Indies, the Indies were kingdoms or provinces incorporated into the Crown of Castile, with a status comparable to that of the peninsular kingdoms, and not colonies. He bases his thesis on laws of the Recopilación, on the existence of audiencias and cabildos, and on the fact that the word “colony” became general only with the Bourbons of the 18th century.

fuentes/las-indias-no-eran-colonias/por_.texto: His thesis had great influence on Argentine legal historiography. Its critics point out that the formal equality among kingdoms did not prevent economic and political subordination or the servile condition of Indigenous people and slaves.

fuentes/la-leyenda-negra-garcia-carcel/t.texto: The Black Legend: History and Opinion

fuentes/la-leyenda-negra-garcia-carcel/r.texto: Study by the Spanish historian Ricardo García Cárcel on how the negative image of Spain was formed and changed between the 16th and 20th centuries, and on the Spanish responses to it. It distinguishes the propaganda of rivals from internal criticism and shows that many arguments of the black legend originated in Spain itself, such as those of Las Casas.

fuentes/la-leyenda-negra-garcia-carcel/p.texto: It represents the Spanish academic historiography that recognizes the existence of anti-Spanish propaganda but does not use it to deny documented facts.

fuentes/white-legend-revisited/titulo.texto: The White Legend Revisited: A Reply to Professor Hanke’s “Modest Proposal”

fuentes/white-legend-revisited/soporte.texto: Article in the Hispanic American Historical Review

fuentes/white-legend-revisited/resumen.texto: Benjamin Keen’s reply to Lewis Hanke’s proposal for a moratorium. He argues that, by putting the protective laws and the debates of the theologians in the foreground, Hanke and other historians built a “white legend” of the conquest as partial as the black one, and that the condition of Indigenous people should be judged by practices and not by norms.

fuentes/white-legend-revisited/por_que_i.texto: It closed the exchange between the two historians and gave its name to the critique of the apologetic view of the conquest.

fuentes/imperiofobia/titulo.texto: Imperiophobia and the Black Legend: Rome, Russia, the United States and the Spanish Empire

fuentes/imperiofobia/resumen.texto: Essay that interprets the black legend as a case of “imperiophobia,” the propaganda that empires generate among their rivals and their own elites, and compares it with those of Rome, Russia and the United States. It attributes the legend against Spain above all to Protestant propaganda, especially German and Dutch, and to anticatholicism.

fuentes/imperiofobia/por_que_importa.texto: It was a bestseller and reopened the public debate in Spain and America. Historians and philosophers such as José Luis Villacañas objected to its errors, selective use of sources and an apologetic tone that minimizes the violence of the conquest.

fuentes/imperiofilia/resumen.texto: Critical response to Imperiofobia in which Villacañas argues that Roca Barea’s book handles sources badly, confuses historical criticism with propaganda and reproduces a national-Catholic vision of Spanish history useful to contemporary political populism.

fuentes/imperiofilia/por_que_importa.texto: It is one of the main academic criticisms of the recent vindication of the Spanish Empire and shows that the debate over the black legend still has political content.

fuentes/poblacion-indigena-rosenblat/tit.texto: The Indigenous Population and Mestizaje in America

fuentes/poblacion-indigena-rosenblat/sop.texto: Two volumes (Buenos Aires, Editorial Nova); expands a 1945 version

fuentes/poblacion-indigena-rosenblat/res.texto: Estimate of the Indigenous population of America in 1492 and its evolution up to the 20th century, region by region, based on chronicles, tribute rates and colonial censuses. It calculates some 13.4 million inhabitants for 1492 across the continent.

fuentes/poblacion-indigena-rosenblat/por.texto: It is the main low estimate of the 20th century. Later research, such as that of Cook and Borah or Dobyns, proposed much higher figures, and the debate remains open.

fuentes/poblacion-aborigen-cook-borah/ti.texto: The Aboriginal Population of Central Mexico on the Eve of the Spanish Conquest

fuentes/poblacion-aborigen-cook-borah/au.texto: Sherburne F. Cook and Woodrow Borah

fuentes/poblacion-aborigen-cook-borah/re.texto: Study by the so-called Berkeley school which, based on tribute records, estimates the population of central Mexico at about 25 million in 1518 and follows its decline to just over one million around 1605.

fuentes/poblacion-aborigen-cook-borah/po.texto: It is the basis of the high estimates of the demographic decline. Its critics debate the coefficients used to convert tribute payers into inhabitants.

fuentes/demographic-collapse-cook/titulo.texto: The Demographic Collapse of Indigenous Peru, 1520–1620

fuentes/demographic-collapse-cook/resume.texto: Study of the Indigenous population of Peru from the conquest to 1620, based on visitations, censuses and tribute rates. It estimates about nine million inhabitants around 1520 and some 600,000 in 1620, and attributes the decline mainly to epidemics, aggravated by war, forced labor and social disorganization.

fuentes/demographic-collapse-cook/por_qu.texto: It is the reference estimate for the Andes and shows that the decline was enormous even with the most cautious initial figures.

fuentes/born-to-die/titulo.texto: Born to Die: Disease and the Conquest of the New World, 1492–1650

fuentes/born-to-die/resumen.texto: Synthesis of the epidemics that followed the arrival of the Europeans, such as smallpox, measles, typhus and influenza, with their chronology by region. It argues that disease was the main cause of the demographic catastrophe, without denying the role of violence and exploitation.

fuentes/born-to-die/por_que_importa.texto: It is a reference for the academic consensus on the weight of epidemics. Its critics warn that this emphasis is sometimes used to dilute the responsibility of the conquest.

fuentes/native-population-denevan/titulo.texto: The Native Population of the Americas in 1492

fuentes/native-population-denevan/soport.texto: University of Wisconsin Press; second revised edition 1992

fuentes/native-population-denevan/resume.texto: Collective book that gathers and compares regional estimates of the American population in 1492. In the revised 1992 edition, Denevan proposes a total of some 54 million, between the low figures of Rosenblat and the high ones of Dobyns.

fuentes/native-population-denevan/por_qu.texto: His consensus figure is the most cited in general works.

fuentes/estimating-aboriginal-dobyns/tit.texto: Estimating the Aboriginal Population of the Americas

fuentes/estimating-aboriginal-dobyns/sop.texto: Article in the journal Current Anthropology

fuentes/estimating-aboriginal-dobyns/res.texto: Article that criticizes the low estimates of the American population and, assuming that epidemics reduced the population in similar proportions across the continent, proposes for 1492 between 90 and 112 million inhabitants.

fuentes/estimating-aboriginal-dobyns/por.texto: It opened the debate about high figures. Many specialists consider that his method excessively multiplied the minimum recorded populations.

fuentes/los-estragos-de-la-conquista/tit.texto: The Ravages of the Conquest: Decline and Fall of the Indians of America

fuentes/los-estragos-de-la-conquista/res.texto: Study by an Italian demographer of the decline of the Indigenous population in the Caribbean, Mexico and the Andes. He argues that epidemics do not suffice to explain it and that the disarticulation of communities, forced labor, displacements and the appropriation of women by the conquistadors also weighed.

fuentes/los-estragos-de-la-conquista/por.texto: It represents the current that, without denying the epidemics, restores weight to the social and political factors of the conquest.

fuentes/trata-de-negros-studer/titulo.texto: The Slave Trade in the Río de la Plata in the 18th Century

fuentes/trata-de-negros-studer/resumen.texto: Documentary study of the introduction of African slaves through Buenos Aires and Montevideo during the 18th century: the French and British asientos, the registro ships and the opening of the trade at the end of the period. It gathers figures of arrivals and sales from customs and company records.

fuentes/trata-de-negros-studer/por_que_i.texto: It is the reference work on the slave trade in the Río de la Plata, and its series are the basis of many later estimates.

fuentes/censo-de-1778/titulo.texto: Census of Buenos Aires and the Viceroyalty of 1778

fuentes/censo-de-1778/autor.texto: Government of Viceroy Juan José de Vértiz

fuentes/censo-de-1778/resumen.texto: Population count taken in 1778 in the newly created viceroyalty, which classified inhabitants by their “quality”: Spaniards, Indians, mestizos, mulattoes and Blacks, free or enslaved. In the city of Buenos Aires it recorded about 24,000 inhabitants, of whom nearly 30% were noted as Black or mulatto. The total of the censused jurisdictions, without Corrientes or Santa Fe, came to around 180,000 to 190,000 inhabitants. In those of Tucumán the proportion of Black and mulatto people was higher: according to the published summaries, which vary from one author to another, more than half in Santiago del Estero and Catamarca and more than 40% in Salta, Córdoba and Tucumán.

fuentes/censo-de-1778/por_que_importa.texto: It is the main source on the African and Afro-descendant population at the end of the colonial period. The categories depended on the criterion of the enumerator and changed from one register to another, so the figures are useful as orders of magnitude.

fuentes/censo-de-1778/leer.0.titulo.texto: Documentos para la historia argentina, tomo XI (Facultad de Filosofía y Letras, 1919), on Internet Archive

fuentes/dominus-ac-redemptor-1773/resume.texto: Brief of July 21, 1773, by which Clement XIV suppressed the Society of Jesus throughout the Church. It reviews the orders that earlier popes had suppressed and argues that the Society had been beset from its beginnings by disputes, internal and with bishops, other religious orders and civil authorities in Europe, Asia and America, which in some places had led to tumults. It declares the Society suppressed in order to restore peace to the Church.

fuentes/dominus-ac-redemptor-1773/por_qu.texto: Six years after the expulsion of the Jesuits from the Spanish domains, which had ended the Jesuit administration of the Río de la Plata missions, the bull put an end to the order almost everywhere in the world until its universal restoration by Pius VII in 1814. The Bourbon courts had requested it, the ambassador Moñino pressed the pope, and Charles III rewarded him with the title of Count of Floridablanca.

fuentes/dominus-ac-redemptor-1773/leer.0.texto: Introduction and English translation of the brief by John Murphy, S.J., in McCoog (ed.), 2003, on the Portal to Jesuit Studies (Boston College)

personas/juan-diaz-de-solis/resumen.texto: Navigator of disputed origin, born in Lebrija or in Portugal depending on the authors, and chief pilot of Castile from 1512. In 1516 he entered with three ships the estuary he called Mar Dulce, later the Río de la Plata, and died on the eastern coast at the hands of Indigenous people; the survivors returned to Spain.

personas/fernando-de-magallanes/resumen.texto: Portuguese navigator in the service of Castile who led the expedition that crossed the strait that bears his name (1520). He wintered at San Julián, where he put down a mutiny, and died at Mactan (Philippines) in 1521; Juan Sebastián Elcano completed the circumnavigation.

personas/sebastian-caboto/resumen.texto: Chief pilot of Castile who in 1526 set out for the Moluccas and changed course toward the Río de la Plata, attracted by reports of silver. He founded Fort Sancti Spíritus (1527) and went up the Paraná and the Paraguay; he returned to Spain in 1530 and was prosecuted for disobeying his instructions.

personas/diego-garcia-de-moguer/resumen.texto: Andalusian pilot who had sailed with Solís. He reached the Río de la Plata in 1528 at the head of a private expedition, found Cabot’s fort on the Paraná and ended up joining him.

personas/pedro-de-mendoza/resumen.texto: Nobleman from Guadix who signed in 1534 the capitulation with Charles V to conquer the Río de la Plata. His expedition, one of the largest sent to the Río de la Plata, founded the settlement of Santa María del Buen Ayre in 1536; ill, he returned to Spain and died on the voyage in 1537.

personas/juan-de-ayolas/resumen.texto: Lieutenant of Pedro de Mendoza, who named him his successor. He went up the Paraná and the Paraguay, entered the Chaco in search of the Sierra de la Plata and died at the hands of the Payaguás on his return, around 1538.

personas/juan-de-salazar-de-espinosa/res.texto: Captain of the Mendoza expedition who in August 1537 raised the fortified house of Nuestra Señora de la Asunción, origin of the city of Asunción.

personas/alvar-nunez-cabeza-de-vaca/resu.texto: Survivor of the Narváez expedition in North America (1527–1536), recounted in his Naufragios. As adelantado of the Río de la Plata he reached Asunción overland from the coast of Brazil (1541–1542) and saw the Iguazú falls. The royal officials and residents deposed him in 1544 and sent him prisoner to Spain, where he was prosecuted.

personas/domingo-martinez-de-irala/resum.texto: Basque from the Mendoza expedition, elected governor by the conquerors of Asunción under a royal decree of 1537. He ordered the depopulation of Buenos Aires (1541), governed Paraguay almost without interruption until his death and in 1556 distributed the Guaraníes in encomiendas. In his will he acknowledged the children he had with several Guaraní women.

personas/isabel-de-guevara/resumen.texto: Woman from the Pedro de Mendoza expedition. In 1556 she wrote from Asunción to Princess Juana a letter describing the hunger of the first Buenos Aires and the work of the women of the expedition, and asking for a repartimiento for herself and her husband.

personas/nuflo-de-chaves/resumen.texto: Conquistador from Extremadura who explored, from Asunción, the Chaco and the east of present-day Bolivia, where he founded Santa Cruz de la Sierra in 1561. He died in an Indigenous attack in 1568.

personas/diego-de-rojas/resumen.texto: Led the first Spanish expedition into the present-day northwest of Argentina (1543–1546), departing from Cusco and Charcas. He died in 1544 from a poisoned arrow; his men continued as far as the ruins of Sancti Spíritus before returning to Peru.

personas/juan-nunez-de-prado/resumen.texto: Sent from Charcas by Pedro de la Gasca, he founded in 1550 the city of El Barco, the first in Tucumán, which he moved several times. Francisco de Aguirre, who arrived from Chile, arrested him and displaced him in 1553.

personas/francisco-de-aguirre/resumen.texto: Captain of Pedro de Valdivia in Chile. In 1553 he moved the city of El Barco and gave it the name Santiago del Estero; he was governor of Tucumán, and the Inquisition prosecuted him for statements considered heretical, which he had to abjure in 1569.

personas/juan-perez-de-zurita/resumen.texto: Lieutenant governor of Tucumán appointed from Chile. He founded London (1558), Córdoba de Calchaquí (1559), Cañete (1560) and Nieva (1561), which did not survive the uprising of the Calchaquí peoples in the following years.

personas/pedro-del-castillo/resumen.texto: Captain sent by the governor of Chile, García Hurtado de Mendoza, who on March 2, 1561 founded the city of Mendoza del Nuevo Valle de La Rioja, on Huarpe land.

personas/juan-jufre/nombre.texto: Juan Jufré de Loaysa y Montesa

personas/juan-jufre/resumen.texto: Conqueror of Chile who in 1562 moved Mendoza to a nearby site and founded San Juan de la Frontera. He died in Santiago de Chile.

personas/garcia-hurtado-de-mendoza/resum.texto: Governor of Chile (1557–1561) who ordered the conquest of Cuyo; the city of Mendoza bears his surname. He later served as viceroy of Peru (1590–1596).

personas/diego-de-villarroel/resumen.texto: Nephew of Francisco de Aguirre. On May 31, 1565 he founded San Miguel de Tucumán at the site of Ibatín.

personas/jeronimo-luis-de-cabrera/resume.texto: Governor of Tucumán who founded Córdoba on July 6, 1573 and sought an outlet to the Paraná, where he met Juan de Garay. His successor, Gonzalo de Abreu, had him prosecuted and executed in 1574.

personas/hernando-de-lerma/resumen.texto: Governor of Tucumán who founded the city of Salta, in the Lerma valley, on April 16, 1582.

personas/juan-torres-de-vera-y-aragon/no.texto: Juan Torres de Vera y Aragón

personas/juan-torres-de-vera-y-aragon/re.texto: Judge of the Audiencia of Charcas who, through his marriage to the heiress of Juan Ortiz de Zárate, became adelantado of the Río de la Plata. On April 3, 1588 he founded San Juan de Vera de las Siete Corrientes.

personas/juan-ramirez-de-velasco/resumen.texto: Governor of Tucumán who founded Todos los Santos de la Nueva Rioja on May 20, 1591; he later was governor of the Río de la Plata.

personas/francisco-de-arganaraz/resumen.texto: Founded San Salvador de Velasco in the Jujuy valley on April 19, 1593, after two failed attempts by other captains.

personas/luis-jufre-de-loaysa/nombre.texto: Luis Jufré de Loaysa y Meneses

personas/luis-jufre-de-loaysa/resumen.texto: Deputy corregidor of Cuyo, son of Juan Jufré. Tradition credits him with founding San Luis in 1594, although the record of the act was lost and the date is disputed.

personas/fernando-de-mendoza-mate-de-lun.texto: Fernando de Mendoza Mate de Luna
San Fernando del Valle de Catamarca
Governor of Tucumán who on July 5, 1683 founded San Fernando del Valle de Catamarca, after several failed settlements in the region.

personas/hernandarias/resumen.texto: Creole born in Asunción, considered the first American-born person to hold office in the Spanish Indies: he governed the Río de la Plata and Paraguay in several periods between 1592 and 1618. He pursued smuggling, promoted the Jesuit and Franciscan reductions and proposed dividing the governorship, which the Crown did in 1617.

personas/jose-de-garro/resumen.texto: Governor of Buenos Aires who in August 1680 ordered the storming of the Colonia del Sacramento, recently founded by the Portuguese. The provisional Treaty of Lisbon (1681) disapproved the action and demanded its cessation; the following year he went on to govern Chile (1682–1692).

personas/manuel-lobo/resumen.texto: Portuguese governor of Rio de Janeiro who founded the Colonia del Sacramento in January 1680. He was captured in the Spanish assault of August and died as a prisoner in Buenos Aires.

personas/bruno-mauricio-de-zabala/resume.texto: Governor of Buenos Aires (1717–1734) who in 1724 dislodged the Portuguese from the bay of Montevideo and founded there the city of San Felipe y Santiago between 1724 and 1726. In 1735 he entered Asunción and ended the Comunero Revolution.

personas/jose-de-antequera/resumen.texto: Judge of Charcas born in Panama, sent as a judge to Paraguay in 1721. He deposed the governor, governed with the support of the Asunción cabildo and confronted the viceroy’s troops; he was tried and executed in Lima in 1731.

personas/francisco-de-paula-bucareli/nom.texto: Francisco de Paula Bucareli y Ursúa

personas/francisco-de-paula-bucareli/res.texto: Governor of Buenos Aires who in 1767 and 1768 carried out the expulsion of the Jesuits from the Río de la Plata, Tucumán and the missions. In 1770 an expedition he sent dislodged the British from the Malvinas Islands.

personas/fernando-de-trejo/resumen.texto: Creole Franciscan, bishop of Tucumán from 1595. In 1613 he pledged to donate his property so that the Jesuits of Córdoba could offer higher studies, the origin of the University of Córdoba.

personas/ignacio-duarte-y-quiros/resumen.texto: Priest born in Córdoba who in 1687 donated his property to the Jesuits to found the Real Colegio Convictorio de Nuestra Señora de Monserrat.

personas/luis-de-bolanos/resumen.texto: Andalusian Franciscan who arrived in Paraguay in 1575. He translated the catechism into Guaraní and founded the first Franciscan villages of Guaraní Indians, precursors of the Jesuit reductions.

personas/antonio-ruiz-de-montoya/resumen.texto: Jesuit born in Lima, missionary in Guairá. In 1631 and 1632 he led south thousands of Guaraníes fleeing the São Paulo bandeirantes. In Madrid he published the Conquista espiritual and the Tesoro de la lengua guaraní (1639) and defended the reductions before the Court.

personas/roque-gonzalez-de-santa-cruz/re.texto: Jesuit born in Asunción who founded several Guaraní reductions between the Paraná and the Uruguay. He was killed at Caaró in 1628, together with another Jesuit, on the orders of a cacique opposed to the missions; the Catholic Church canonized him in 1988.

personas/francisco-de-alfaro/resumen.texto: Judge of the Audiencia of Charcas who visited Paraguay, the Río de la Plata and Tucumán between 1610 and 1612. His ordinances prohibited the personal service of Indigenous people and set a tribute, and they clashed with the resistance of the encomenderos.

personas/buenaventura-suarez/resumen.texto: Jesuit born in Santa Fe who set up an astronomical observatory in the reduction of San Cosme y Damián, with instruments built in the missions. He published a Lunario de un siglo with calculations of the phases of the Moon and of eclipses.

personas/sepe-tiaraju/activo.lugar.texto: San Miguel Arcángel (São Miguel das Missões)

personas/sepe-tiaraju/resumen.texto: Guaraní leader of the San Miguel reduction who led the resistance against the relocation of the Seven Peoples ordered by the Treaty of Madrid. He died in combat on February 7, 1756, three days before the battle of Caibaté; in southern Brazil he is remembered as a hero and a popular saint.

personas/ruy-diaz-de-guzman/resumen.texto: Mestizo born in Asunción, grandson of Irala, soldier and founder of villages in Paraguay. He wrote La Argentina, the first history of the conquest of the Río de la Plata written by someone born in the region, completed in 1612.

personas/martin-del-barco-centenera/resu.texto: Priest from Extremadura who arrived with the Juan Ortiz de Zárate expedition (1573) and traveled through Paraguay, Tucumán and Peru. His poem La Argentina (Lisbon, 1602) is the first printed book to use that name for the region.

personas/pedro-lozano/resumen.texto: Jesuit from Madrid, official chronicler of the Jesuit province of Paraguay. He wrote a description of the Gran Chaco (1733), the history of the Society in the province and a history of the conquest of Paraguay, the Río de la Plata and Tucumán, which was published only in the 19th century.

personas/charlevoix/resumen.texto: French Jesuit and traveler in New France, who wrote a History of Paraguay (1756) based on the Society’s documents, without having been to South America.

personas/martin-dobrizhoffer/resumen.texto: Austrian Jesuit, missionary among the Abipones and the Guaraníes for about eighteen years. After the expulsion he wrote the History of the Abipones (1784) in Vienna.

personas/florian-paucke/resumen.texto: Silesian Jesuit, missionary among the Mocoví people in the San Javier reduction, north of Santa Fe. After the expulsion he wrote an illustrated chronicle with his own watercolors, known in Spanish as Hacia allá y para acá.

personas/ludovico-antonio-muratori/resum.texto: Italian scholar who published Il cristianesimo felice (1743–1749), a eulogy of the Jesuit missions of Paraguay written from letters by missionaries, without having visited them.

personas/alonso-carrio-de-la-vandera/res.texto: Spanish official who inspected the mail between Buenos Aires and Lima (1771–1773). He recounted that journey in El lazarillo de ciegos caminantes, published under the pseudonym Concolorcorvo.

personas/antonio-de-montesinos/resumen.texto: Dominican friar who in December 1511, in Santo Domingo, preached in the name of his community against the treatment that the encomenderos gave Indigenous people. The reaction led to the junta that drafted the Laws of Burgos.

personas/bartolome-de-las-casas/resumen.texto: Encomendero in Hispaniola and Cuba who gave up his Indians in 1514, became a Dominican and was bishop of Chiapas. He denounced the conquest before the Crown, influenced the New Laws, debated Sepúlveda at Valladolid and wrote the Brevísima relación (1552), later used by propaganda against Spain.

personas/francisco-de-vitoria/resumen.texto: Professor of theology at Salamanca. In his 1539 lectures (relecciones) he rejected several titles used to justify the conquest, such as the papal donation or the universal lordship of the emperor, and proposed others based on the law of nations. He is considered a precursor of international law.

personas/juan-gines-de-sepulveda/resumen.texto: Humanist from Córdoba, translator of Aristotle and chronicler of Charles V. He defended the lawfulness of war against Indigenous peoples with the theory of natural servitude and upheld it against Las Casas at the Valladolid junta.

personas/juan-lopez-de-palacios-rubios/r.texto: Jurist of the Council of Castile who took part in the junta of Burgos and drafted the Requerimiento (1513), the text the conquistadors had to read to Indigenous people before waging war on them.

personas/carlos-v/resumen.texto: King of Castile and Aragon from 1516 and emperor from 1519. During his reign the capitulation of Pedro de Mendoza (1534) and the New Laws (1542) were signed, and the Valladolid junta met (1550–1551).

personas/felipe-ii/muerte.lugar.texto: Royal Monastery of San Lorenzo de El Escorial

personas/felipe-ii/resumen.texto: King of Spain from 1556. He created the Audiencia of Charcas (1559) and the governorship of Tucumán (1563), and signed the Ordinances on discovery and settlement of 1573. The propaganda of his Dutch and English enemies fed the black legend.

personas/alejandro-vi/resumen.texto: Valencian pope, Rodrigo Borgia. His bulls of 1493, among them Inter caetera, granted to the Catholic Monarchs the lands discovered and to be discovered west of a line in the Atlantic.

personas/paulo-iii/resumen.texto: Pope who in 1537 promulgated the bull Sublimis Deus, which declared the American Indigenous peoples rational beings, capable of receiving the faith and entitled to their liberty and their property.

personas/juan-de-solorzano/resumen.texto: Jurist who was a judge in Lima and councillor of the Indies. He wrote De Indiarum iure (1629–1639) and Política indiana (1647), the most complete exposition of the law of the Indies, and worked on compiling its laws.

personas/antonio-de-leon-pinelo/resumen.texto: Jurist and bibliographer from a Portuguese converso family, who spent his youth in the Río de la Plata, Tucumán and Lima. In Madrid he prepared a project to compile the Laws of the Indies, which served as the basis for the 1680 compilation.

personas/blasco-nunez-vela/resumen.texto: First viceroy of Peru, who arrived in 1544 to enforce the New Laws. The encomenderos rebelled under Gonzalo Pizarro, the Audiencia deposed him, and he died in the Battle of Iñaquito (1546).

personas/pedro-de-la-gasca/resumen.texto: Cleric and jurist sent to Peru as president of the Audiencia. He defeated Gonzalo Pizarro at Jaquijahuana (1548), moderated the enforcement of the New Laws, and authorized Núñez de Prado's entry into Tucumán.

personas/manuel-de-amat-y-junyent/resume.texto: Catalan military officer, governor of Chile (1755–1761) and viceroy of Peru between 1761 and 1776. Under his government the expulsion of the Jesuits from Peru was carried out (1767), and the Río de la Plata depended on Lima until shortly after he left office.

personas/theodor-de-bry/resumen.texto: Protestant engraver and publisher from Liège, established in Frankfurt. He published the travel collection America (from 1590) and in 1598 a Latin edition of Las Casas’ A Short Account of the Destruction of the Indies with engravings of atrocities that were reproduced for centuries.

personas/julian-juderias/resumen.texto: Spanish essayist who, in The Black Legend and Historical Truth (1914), popularized the expression “black legend” for the hostile image of Spain abroad.

personas/romulo-carbia/resumen.texto: Argentine historian, author of a critical history of Argentine historiography (1925) and of History of the Spanish American Black Legend (1943), where he argued that the image of the conquest rested on exaggerated or forged texts.

personas/lewis-hanke/resumen.texto: American historian of Latin America. In The Spanish Struggle for Justice in the Conquest of America (1949) he studied Spanish debates over the legitimacy of the conquest and the treatment of Indigenous peoples.

personas/philip-powell/resumen.texto: American historian who, in Tree of Hate (1971), argued that anti-Spanish prejudices inherited from the Black Legend shaped American perceptions of the Hispanic world.

personas/maria-elvira-roca-barea/resumen.texto: Spanish philologist and professor, author of Imperiophobia and the Black Legend (2016), a bestseller that interprets the Black Legend as common propaganda against empires; several historians criticized her method and her apologetic tone.

personas/jose-luis-villacanas/resumen.texto: Spanish philosopher, professor at the Complutense University of Madrid, author of Imperiophilia and National-Catholic Populism (2019), a critique of Roca Barea’s book.

personas/angel-rosenblat/resumen.texto: Philologist born in Poland and trained in Argentina, who later worked in Venezuela. He estimated the Indigenous population of the Americas in 1492 at about 13.4 million, one of the lowest estimates.

personas/noble-david-cook/resumen.texto: American historian, professor at Florida International University, who studied the decline of Peru’s Indigenous population between 1520 and 1620 and the role of epidemics in the conquest of the Americas.

personas/william-denevan/resumen.texto: American geographer who gathered and compared estimates of the American population in 1492 and proposed a consensus figure of about 54 million.

personas/henry-dobyns/resumen.texto: American anthropologist who in 1966 proposed that the American population in 1492 was around 90 to 112 million, one of the highest estimates.

personas/felipe-iii/resumen.texto: King of Spain and of Portugal (as Philip II) from 1598 until his death in 1621; he delegated much of the government to his favorite, the Duke of Lerma. A royal decree of his, dated December 16, 1617, divided the governorship of the Río de la Plata and Paraguay, and during his reign the trade permits for Buenos Aires of 1602 and the register ships (navíos de registro) of 1618 were authorized.

personas/juan-ortiz-de-zarate/resumen.texto: Basque from Orduña who went to Peru in 1534 and amassed a fortune as encomendero of Totora and as a miner in Potosí. Appointed interim governor of the Río de la Plata and Paraguay in 1567 by the authority of Peru, and adelantado by Philip II in 1569, he reached the Río de la Plata in 1573 with a fleet, was aided by Juan de Garay against the Charrúa, and entered Asunción in 1575. He died in January 1576 without his daughter Juana having married. His will left the adelantazgo to whoever married her, and his nephew Diego Ortiz de Zárate y Mendieta governed as interim governor (1576–1577). Juan Torres de Vera y Aragón became adelantado after marrying Juana.

personas/francisco-solano/resumen.texto: Andalusian Franciscan friar who went to Peru in 1589 and was assigned to the governorship of Tucumán, where he preached to Indigenous people and settlers and, according to his biographies, also in the Chaco and Paraguay. He was summoned back to Lima in 1595, according to the Diccionario biográfico de la Real Academia de la Historia and García Oro (1988), and died there in 1610. He was beatified in 1675 and canonized in 1726. La Rioja tradition links him to the origin of the Tinkunaco, the rite of the Niño Alcalde of La Rioja.

personas/juan-del-castillo/muerte.lugar.texto: Yjuhí, now Rio Grande do Sul

personas/juan-del-castillo/resumen.texto: Jesuit from Belmonte (Cuenca) who arrived in Buenos Aires in 1617 and studied in Córdoba. Ordained a priest in 1625, between 1626 and 1628 he worked with Roque González in the Guaraní reductions, in charge of the one at Ijuí. He was killed on 17 November 1628 at Yjuhí by Guaraní of the cacique Ñezú, who opposed the missions, two days after Roque González and Alonso Rodríguez were killed. He was beatified in 1934 and canonized in 1988 together with them.

personas/domenico-zipoli/resumen.texto: Baroque composer from Prato, organist of the Gesù church in Rome. In 1716 he joined the Jesuits as a novice in Seville, and in 1717 he arrived in Buenos Aires with other missionaries. He studied in Córdoba and was a musician at the Jesuit church, but he was never ordained for lack of a bishop. He died there in 1726. His religious music was copied for the reductions, and scores by him were found in 1972 in Chiquitos (Bolivia).

personas/esteban-gomez/resumen.texto: Portuguese pilot in the service of Castile. As pilot of the San Antonio in Magellan's fleet he mutinied against his captain near the strait and returned to Seville in May 1521, where he was tried. In 1524–1525 he explored the Atlantic coast of North America. In 1535 he joined Pedro de Mendoza's expedition to the Río de la Plata and died in the spring of 1538 with the column of Juan de Ayolas, ambushed by Indigenous people on the banks of the Paraguay River while returning from the Chaco, according to Vigneras in the Dictionary of Canadian Biography (approximate location). A widely circulated version credits him with sighting the Falklands in 1520; the trial over his desertion does not mention it.

personas/toribio-de-mogrovejo/resumen.texto: Jurist from Mayorga (Valladolid), named archbishop of Lima in 1579 on the proposal of Philip II; he arrived in Lima in 1581. He presided over the Third Council of Lima (1582–1583), which ordered preaching in Indigenous languages and approved the trilingual catechism of 1584, and in 1591 he founded the seminary of Lima. As metropolitan archbishop of Lima he had the dioceses of Tucumán and Paraguay within his ecclesiastical province. The bishop of Tucumán, Francisco de Victoria, went to the Council and opposed him, and Luis de Bolaños translated the catechism into Guaraní, which the 1603 synod of Asunción adopted. He died in Zaña in 1606 during a pastoral visit and was canonized in 1726.

personas/diego-de-almagro/resumen.texto: Castilian conquistador, partner of Francisco Pizarro in the conquest of Peru. His expedition to Chile left Cusco in 1535 and was the first European entry into present-day northwestern Argentina: it passed through Tupiza, the old Chicoana and El Shincal, and crossed the Andes in the autumn of 1536. Defeated by the Pizarros at Las Salinas, he was executed in Cusco in 1538.

personas/antonio-de-guill-y-gonzaga/resu.texto: Governor and captain general of Chile from 1762 to 1768. Since Cuyo depended on Chile, he enforced there the expulsion of the Jesuits of 1767 from the colleges of Mendoza, San Juan and San Luis, which belonged to the Jesuit province of Chile.

hechos/casa-de-contratacion/titulo.texto: Creation of the Casa de Contratación in Seville

hechos/casa-de-contratacion/resumen.texto: The Catholic Monarchs created the Casa de Contratación in Seville in 1503 to control the traffic of people and merchandise with America, which had to pass through that port. Its chief pilot examined pilots and kept the padrón of navigational charts; Amerigo Vespucci, Juan Díaz de Solís and Sebastián Caboto held that post. It moved to Cádiz in 1717.

hechos/tratado-de-tordesillas-hecho/resu.texto: Castile and Portugal divided the lands yet to be discovered with a meridian 370 leagues west of Cape Verde, which moved west the line of the 1493 bull Inter caetera. The line left Brazil to Portugal and was the starting point of the boundary disputes in the Plata basin.

hechos/junta-de-burgos/resumen.texto: Ferdinand the Catholic gathered theologians and jurists in Burgos to respond to complaints from the Dominicans of Hispaniola. The junta affirmed that the Indigenous peoples were free but could be compelled to work and had to be instructed in the faith, and from it came the Laws of Burgos of December 27, 1512.

hechos/consejo-de-indias/titulo.texto: Creation of the Council of the Indies

hechos/consejo-de-indias/resumen.texto: Charles V created the Royal and Supreme Council of the Indies in 1524. It drafted the laws, proposed appointments and judged, in last instance, matters concerning America. It accompanied the court until it settled in Madrid and operated until the 19th century.

hechos/virreinato-del-peru/titulo.texto: Viceroyalty of Peru and its jurisdiction over the Río de la Plata

hechos/virreinato-del-peru/resumen.texto: Created by the New Laws of 1542, with its capital in Lima, it initially covered all of Spanish South America. The governorships of the Río de la Plata, Paraguay and Tucumán depended on it, through the Audiencia of Charcas, until the creation of the Viceroyalty of the Río de la Plata in 1776.

hechos/rebelion-de-gonzalo-pizarro/resum.texto: The encomenderos of Peru rose against the New Laws, which stripped them of the inheritance of their encomiendas, and chose Gonzalo Pizarro as their leader. They defeated and killed Viceroy Blasco Núñez Vela at Iñaquito (1546). Pedro de la Gasca arrived with the revocation of the most resisted clauses, defeated Pizarro at Jaquijahuana in 1548, and had him executed.

hechos/junta-de-valladolid/resumen.texto: Charles V ordered the suspension of new conquests and convened in Valladolid a junta of theologians and jurists to decide how they could be carried out justly. Sepúlveda defended war against the Indigenous peoples on account of their supposed natural servitude, and Las Casas argued that they were rational peoples who could only be drawn to the faith by peaceful means. The sessions of 1550 and 1551 ended without a formal ruling.

hechos/inquisicion-de-lima/titulo.texto: Tribunal of the Inquisition of Lima

hechos/inquisicion-de-lima/resumen.texto: Philip II created the Holy Office tribunal of Lima in 1569. It began operating in 1570 with jurisdiction over the entire viceroyalty of Peru, including Tucumán and the Río de la Plata, where it acted through commissioners. Indigenous people fell outside its jurisdiction; its cases mainly targeted Portuguese Jewish conversos, Protestants, bigamists, and those accused of sorcery or heretical propositions.

hechos/tercer-concilio-limense/resumen.texto: Provincial council convened by Archbishop Toribio de Mogrovejo with the bishops of the viceroyalty, including the bishop of Tucumán. It approved a single catechism in Castilian, Quechua and Aymara, printed in Lima in 1584 as the first book of South America, and ordered the priests of Indians to preach in Indigenous languages.

hechos/cabildos-coloniales/titulo.texto: The cabildos of the colonial cities

hechos/cabildos-coloniales/resumen.texto: Each founded city had a cabildo made up of alcaldes, who acted as first-instance judges, and regidores, initially chosen by the founder and later by the councillors themselves or bought from the Crown, which from the late 16th century sold these posts. The cabildos governed the city and its countryside, distributed land and urban plots, and in grave cases summoned the leading residents to a cabildo abierto. In Buenos Aires it operated from Garay’s founding in 1580 until the provincial legislature abolished it in 1821.

hechos/viaje-de-solis/titulo.texto: Juan Díaz de Solís’s voyage to the Río de la Plata

hechos/viaje-de-solis/resumen.texto: Expedition of three ships that left Sanlúcar de Barrameda in October 1515 in search of a passage to the Pacific Ocean. In early 1516 it entered the estuary, which he called Mar Dulce, and Solís died with several men when they landed on the eastern shore, attacked by Indigenous people. Later chroniclers claimed the attackers ate them, something historians dispute; the survivors returned to Spain, and some castaways remained on the Brazilian coast.

hechos/viaje-de-magallanes/resumen.texto: Expedition of five ships in the service of Castile, seeking a route to the Spice Islands by the west. It explored the Río de la Plata and the Patagonian coast, crossed in 1520 the strait that bears Magellan’s name, and crossed the Pacific. After Magellan’s death in the Philippines, a single ship, under Juan Sebastián Elcano, returned to Spain in 1522 with 18 men.
