hechos/invernada-en-san-julian/titulo.texto: Winter camp and mutiny at San Julián

hechos/invernada-en-san-julian/resumen.texto: Magellan’s expedition spent the 1520 austral winter in San Julián Bay. There it suppressed a mutiny of Castilian captains: Luis de Mendoza died in the fighting, Gaspar de Quesada was executed, and Juan de Cartagena and a priest were abandoned on the coast. The expedition had its first contacts with the Tehuelches, whom Pigafetta described as giants and whom, according to his account, Magellan called patagones.

hechos/fuerte-sancti-spiritus/resumen.texto: Sebastián Caboto, who had left the route to the Moluccas drawn by reports of a sierra rich in silver, built on June 9, 1527 Fort Sancti Spíritus at the mouth of the Carcarañá, the first Spanish settlement in present-day Argentine territory. From there he went up the Paraná and the Paraguay. In 1529 an Indigenous attack destroyed the fort, and the expedition returned to Spain in 1530.

hechos/expedicion-de-diego-garcia/titulo.texto: Expedition of Diego García de Moguer

hechos/expedicion-de-diego-garcia/resume.texto: Private expedition that left A Coruña in 1527 and reached the Río de la Plata in February 1528. On the Paraná it found Caboto’s fort; García disputed jurisdiction with him and then joined him in exploring the Paraná and the Paraguay.

hechos/despoblamiento-de-buenos-aires/ti.texto: Abandonment of the first Buenos Aires

hechos/despoblamiento-de-buenos-aires/re.texto: Domingo Martínez de Irala, governor from Asunción, ordered the abandonment of the Buenos Aires settlement, which had failed to sustain itself because of hunger and clashes with the Querandí. Its residents moved to Asunción in 1541, and the Río de la Plata coast remained without a stable Spanish population until 1580.

hechos/viaje-de-alvar-nunez/resumen.texto: The adelantado Álvar Núñez Cabeza de Vaca landed on Santa Catalina Island, off the Brazilian coast, and marched overland with Guaraní guides to Asunción, arriving in March 1542. Along the way he saw the Iguazú Falls, of which he left the earliest known European mention.

hechos/deposicion-de-alvar-nunez/titulo.texto: Deposition of Álvar Núñez Cabeza de Vaca

hechos/deposicion-de-alvar-nunez/resumen.texto: In April 1544 the royal officials and residents of Asunción arrested the adelantado, accused him of abuses and of governing against the conquistadors, and returned the government to Irala. In 1545 they sent him to Spain as a prisoner. The Commentaries of Álvar Núñez presents him as a protector of Indigenous peoples against the abuses of the residents, while Schmidl and his adversaries described him as an arbitrary ruler.

hechos/repartimiento-de-irala/titulo.texto: Irala assigns Guaraní peoples to encomiendas

hechos/repartimiento-de-irala/resumen.texto: In 1556 Governor Domingo Martínez de Irala distributed the Guaraní of the Asunción region among the residents in encomiendas, shortly before his death. The earlier relationship between Spaniards and Guaraní, based on alliances and on the kinship created by Guaraní women given to the conquistadors, became a system of compulsory personal service.

hechos/fundacion-de-santa-cruz-de-la-sie.texto: Founding of Santa Cruz de la Sierra
Ñuflo de Chaves, who had set out from Asunción, founded Santa Cruz de la Sierra on February 26, 1561, on the eastern plains of present-day Bolivia, on the route between Paraguay and Peru.

hechos/entrada-de-diego-de-rojas/titulo.texto: Diego de Rojas’s expedition to Tucumán

hechos/entrada-de-diego-de-rojas/resumen.texto: Expedition of Spaniards and Indigenous auxiliaries that left Peru in 1543 and was the first to traverse present-day northwestern Argentina. Rojas died in 1544, struck by a poisoned arrow. His successors continued to the Paraná, where they found the ruins of Sancti Spíritus, and the survivors returned to Peru in 1546.

hechos/fundacion-de-el-barco/titulo.texto: Núñez de Prado founds El Barco

hechos/fundacion-de-el-barco/resumen.texto: Juan Núñez de Prado, sent from Charcas by Pedro de la Gasca, founded the city of El Barco, the first in Tucumán, on June 29, 1550. The city changed site twice before 1552, and in 1553 Francisco de Aguirre, who had arrested Núñez de Prado, moved it again and named it Santiago del Estero.

hechos/fundacion-de-santiago-del-estero/.texto: On July 25, 1553, Francisco de Aguirre, arriving from Chile, moved the city of El Barco to the bank of the Dulce River and named it Santiago del Estero del Nuevo Maestrazgo. The city dates its origin from 1553, although some historians trace it to the founding of El Barco in 1550.

hechos/fundacion-de-londres/resumen.texto: Juan Pérez de Zurita founded the city of Londres in 1558, named in honor of Philip II’s marriage to Mary Tudor. It was the second city of Tucumán, and the Calchaquí uprisings forced it to move several times.

hechos/fundacion-de-mendoza/resumen.texto: On March 2, 1561, Captain Pedro del Castillo, sent by the governor of Chile García Hurtado de Mendoza, founded the City of Mendoza of the New Valley of La Rioja in Huarpe territory. The following year Juan Jufré moved it to a nearby site.

hechos/fundacion-de-san-juan/resumen.texto: On June 13, 1562, Juan Jufré founded San Juan de la Frontera, in the Tulum valley, in Huarpe territory, as part of the conquest of Cuyo from Chile.

hechos/creacion-de-la-gobernacion-del-tu.texto: Creation of the governorship of Tucumán

A royal decree of Philip II dated August 29, 1563, separated the province of Tucumán, Juríes and Diaguitas from the governorship of Chile and placed it under the Audiencia of Charcas. Its first capital was Santiago del Estero; it covered present-day northwestern Argentina and Córdoba, and in 1782 it was divided into the intendancies of Salta and Córdoba.

hechos/fundacion-de-san-miguel-de-tucuma.texto: Founding of San Miguel de Tucumán

On May 31, 1565, Diego de Villarroel, by order of governor Francisco de Aguirre, founded San Miguel de Tucumán and Nueva Tierra de Promisión at the site of Ibatín. In 1685 the city moved to its present location.

hechos/fundacion-de-cordoba/resumen.texto: On July 6, 1573, the governor of Tucumán, Jerónimo Luis de Cabrera, founded Córdoba de la Nueva Andalucía beside the Suquía River, in the land of the Comechingón and Sanavirón, with the aim of opening an outlet from the governorship to the Río de la Plata.

hechos/fundacion-de-salta/resumen.texto: On April 16, 1582, the governor of Tucumán, Hernando de Lerma, founded the city of Lerma in the Salta valley, to secure the route between Tucumán and Upper Peru against the Calchaquí peoples.

hechos/fundacion-de-la-rioja/resumen.texto: On May 20, 1591, Governor Juan Ramírez de Velasco founded Todos los Santos de la Nueva Rioja, in Diaguita territory, and distributed the Indigenous population among the residents in encomiendas.

hechos/fundacion-de-jujuy/titulo.texto: Founding of San Salvador de Jujuy

hechos/fundacion-de-jujuy/resumen.texto: On April 19, 1593, Francisco de Argañaraz y Murguía founded San Salvador de Velasco in the Jujuy valley, after the settlements of 1561 and 1575 had been destroyed by the peoples of the region.

hechos/fundacion-de-san-luis/resumen.texto: Tradition dates the founding of San Luis de Loyola Nueva Medina de Río Seco to August 25, 1594, by Luis Jufré de Loaysa y Meneses, lieutenant corregidor of Cuyo. The founding act was lost and the city was later moved and refounded, so both the date and the founder are disputed.

hechos/fundacion-de-catamarca/titulo.texto: Founding of San Fernando del Valle de Catamarca

hechos/fundacion-de-catamarca/lugar.texto: San Fernando del Valle de Catamarca

hechos/fundacion-de-catamarca/resumen.texto: On July 5, 1683, the governor of Tucumán, Fernando de Mendoza Mate de Luna, founded San Fernando del Valle de Catamarca, after a century of failed settlements in the region due to Calchaquí resistance.

hechos/traslado-de-san-miguel-de-tucuman.texto: Relocation of San Miguel de Tucumán
In 1685 the city of San Miguel de Tucumán left the site of Ibatín, plagued by floods, diseases and attacks, and settled at La Toma, its present location.

hechos/terremoto-de-esteco/resumen.texto: On September 13, 1692, an earthquake destroyed the city of Talavera de Madrid de Esteco, already in decline, and damaged Salta. In Salta, the devotion to the Señor and the Virgen del Milagro, whose processions are held every September, arose from the prayers offered during those tremors.

hechos/fundacion-de-santa-fe/resumen.texto: On November 15, 1573, Juan de Garay, with residents of Asunción who were mostly mestizos born in Paraguay, founded Santa Fe by the river of the Quiloazas, today San Javier. It was the first step toward resettling the Río de la Plata and giving Asunción an outlet to the Atlantic.

hechos/revolucion-de-los-siete-jefes/res.texto: On May 31 and June 1, 1580, a group of Santa Fe residents, mostly young men born locally (mancebos nacidos en la tierra), deposed lieutenant governor Simón Xaque and the authorities appointed by Garay. One of the participants betrayed the movement, and its ringleaders were executed. Argentine historiography remembers it as the first Creole uprising in the Río de la Plata.

hechos/fundacion-de-concepcion-del-berme.texto: In 1585 Alonso de Vera y Aragón founded the city of Concepción de Nuestra Señora in the Chaco, on the Bermejo River, with residents of Asunción, to link Paraguay with Tucumán. Attacks by Chaco peoples forced its abandonment in 1632.

hechos/fundacion-de-corrientes/resumen.texto: On April 3, 1588, the adelantado Juan Torres de Vera y Aragón founded San Juan de Vera de las Siete Corrientes, near the confluence of the Paraná and the Paraguay, as a stop on the river route between Asunción and Buenos Aires.

hechos/permisos-de-comercio-de-buenos-ai.texto: Trade restrictions and permits through Buenos Aires

To protect the fleet system that ran through Panama and Lima, the Crown did not authorize direct trade between Buenos Aires and Europe or Brazil, except through limited permits. In 1602 it allowed, for six years, the export of small quantities of flour, cecina and tallow, and in 1618 it authorized two registro ships a year. With so little legal trade, smuggling, especially with the Portuguese of Brazil, was a central part of Buenos Aires’ economy in the 17th century, as historian Zacarías Moutoukias showed (1988).

hechos/hospital-de-san-martin-buenos-air.texto: Juan de Garay had set aside a plot for a hospital in 1580, but only on February 4, 1610, did the cabildo order the construction of the Hospital de San Martín, also called del Rey, the city’s first. In 1748 it passed to the Bethlehemite friars, who came from Potosí, and from then on it was called the Hospital de Santa Catalina.

hechos/division-de-la-gobernacion-1617/t.texto: Division of the governorship of the Río de la Plata and Paraguay

hechos/division-de-la-gobernacion-1617/r.texto: A royal decree of Philip III dated December 16, 1617, at the proposal of Hernandarias, divided the governorship in two: that of Guairá or Paraguay, with its capital in Asunción, and that of the Río de la Plata, with its capital in Buenos Aires, which included Santa Fe, Corrientes and Concepción del Bermejo. The first governor of Buenos Aires, Diego de Góngora, took office in 1618.

hechos/aduana-seca-de-cordoba/resumen.texto: To protect Lima’s commercial monopoly and curb smuggling through Buenos Aires, a royal decree of 1622 established an inland customs house in Córdoba that charged a duty on goods moving from the Río de la Plata to Tucumán and Peru. Historiography commonly cites a rate of 50%. Smuggling continued by other routes, and in 1695 the customs house was moved to Jujuy.

hechos/traslado-de-santa-fe/resumen.texto: Because of the river’s floods and attacks by Chaco peoples, the Santa Fe council decided in 1651 to move the city about 80 kilometers south, to its present site. The move was completed around 1660, and the old settlement fell into ruin.

hechos/primera-audiencia-de-buenos-aires.texto: A royal decree of 1661 created an audiencia in Buenos Aires to combat smuggling and defend the port, with jurisdiction over the Río de la Plata, Paraguay and Tucumán. It operated between 1663 and 1672, when it was suppressed and the district again depended on Charcas.

hechos/santa-fe-puerto-preciso/resumen.texto: In 1739 the Audiencia of Charcas ruled that Santa Fe would be a required port, and a royal decree confirmed it in 1743: vessels coming down from Paraguay with yerba mate, tobacco and other products had to unload and pay their duties there. Local histories trace the privilege back to a royal decree of 1662. The privilege pitted the councils of Santa Fe, Asunción and Buenos Aires against one another and was abolished in 1780.

hechos/fundacion-de-colonia-del-sacramen.texto: Founding and capture of Colonia del Sacramento

In January 1680 the Portuguese Manuel Lobo, governor of Rio de Janeiro, founded the Colonia del Sacramento across from Buenos Aires. On August 7, forces sent by governor José de Garro, with thousands of Guaraníes from the missions, took it by storm. The provisional Treaty of Lisbon of 1681 forced its return.

hechos/toma-de-colonia-1705/titulo.texto: Siege and capture of Colonia del Sacramento (1704–1705)

hechos/toma-de-colonia-1705/resumen.texto: During the War of the Spanish Succession, forces from Buenos Aires and the missions besieged Colonia for five months and occupied it in March 1705, after the Portuguese evacuated it by sea. The Treaty of Utrecht forced its return to Portugal in 1715.

hechos/asiento-britanico/titulo.texto: British asiento for enslaved Africans in Buenos Aires

hechos/asiento-britanico/resumen.texto: Under the asiento signed with Great Britain in 1713, the South Sea Company set up a factory in Buenos Aires for the sale of enslaved Africans, with warehouses in the area of present-day Retiro. It operated with interruptions due to wars between the two crowns until the late 1730s, and it was also a channel for British smuggling. Earlier, between 1702 and 1713, the asiento had been in the hands of the French Guinea Company, which also operated in Buenos Aires.

hechos/fundacion-de-montevideo/resumen.texto: In 1724 the governor of Buenos Aires, Bruno Mauricio de Zabala, dislodged the Portuguese who had settled on the bay of Montevideo and built a fort there. Between 1724 and 1726 he founded the city of San Felipe y Santiago de Montevideo with families who came from Buenos Aires and the Canary Islands.

hechos/sitio-de-colonia-1735/resumen.texto: The governor of Buenos Aires, Miguel de Salcedo, besieged Colonia for almost two years without being able to take it, because the Portuguese supplied it by sea. The siege ended with the armistice signed in Paris in 1737.

hechos/toma-de-colonia-1762/titulo.texto: Pedro de Cevallos takes Colonia del Sacramento

hechos/toma-de-colonia-1762/resumen.texto: When Spain entered the Seven Years’ War, the governor of Buenos Aires, Pedro de Cevallos, besieged and took Colonia in October 1762. The Treaty of Paris of 1763 forced its return, and Cevallos occupied it permanently in 1777, by then as viceroy.

hechos/trata-de-esclavos-en-el-rio-de-la.texto: African slave trade through the Río de la Plata

From the late 16th century, enslaved Africans arrived through Buenos Aires under licenses, asientos, or by smuggling from Brazil, and many were taken to Tucumán, Cuyo, Chile and Upper Peru. They worked in domestic service, trades, transport and estancias, including those of the Jesuits. In 1812 the revolutionary government prohibited the introduction of enslaved people, and in 1813 the Assembly declared the children of enslaved women free. Complete abolition came with the Constitution of 1853 and, in Buenos Aires, in 1861.

hechos/segunda-audiencia-de-buenos-aires.texto: Re-establishment of the Audiencia of Buenos Aires

The Audiencia of Buenos Aires was reinstalled in 1785, now as the audiencia of the Viceroyalty of the Río de la Plata, with jurisdiction over the intendancies of Buenos Aires, Córdoba, Salta and Paraguay. It sat in the Cabildo until 1812, when the revolutionary government replaced it with a court of appeals.

hechos/comuneros-del-paraguay/titulo.texto: Revolt of the comuneros of Paraguay

hechos/comuneros-del-paraguay/resumen.texto: In 1721 the oidor José de Antequera, sent to investigate governor Diego de los Reyes Balmaceda, deposed him and governed with the support of the Asunción cabildo, which was at odds with the Jesuits over control of the Indigenous people of the missions. In 1724 Antequera defeated the troops sent by the viceroy, but he was captured and executed in Lima in 1731. The movement continued under Fernando Mompox, who held that the power of the común stood above that of the governor, until Zabala suppressed it in 1735. Historians debate whether it was an antecedent of Creole autonomy or a conflict between residents and Jesuits over Guaraní labor.

hechos/cerro-rico/titulo.texto: Discovery of silver at Cerro Rico of Potosí

hechos/cerro-rico/resumen.texto: In 1545 the first silver veins of Cerro Rico, in Upper Peru, were registered, and at its foot the town of Potosí arose. Its output, the largest in the world at the end of the 16th century, organized the economy of the entire region: Tucumán and the Litoral sold it mules, cattle, textiles and food, and Buenos Aires sought an outlet for its silver.

hechos/audiencia-de-charcas/titulo.texto: Creation of the Audiencia of Charcas

hechos/audiencia-de-charcas/resumen.texto: A royal decree of Philip II of 1559 created the Royal Audiencia of La Plata de los Charcas, which began operating in 1561. It was the high court and governing body on which Tucumán, Paraguay and the Río de la Plata depended for almost the entire colonial period, except during the years of the first Audiencia of Buenos Aires.

hechos/mita-de-potosi/resumen.texto: Viceroy Francisco de Toledo organized the mining mita from 1573. It required the communities of sixteen Andean provinces to send in rotation one-seventh of their adult men to work in the Potosí mines for low wages. It adapted an Inca institution of rotational labor to silver mining, and the Cortes of Cádiz abolished it in 1812. Its legitimacy was already debated in its own time, and historiography counts it among the causes of the flight and population decline of the Andean communities.

hechos/visita-de-alfaro/titulo.texto: Inspection by oidor Francisco de Alfaro

hechos/visita-de-alfaro/resumen.texto: The oidor of Charcas Francisco de Alfaro toured Paraguay, the Río de la Plata and Tucumán to investigate the treatment of Indigenous peoples, and issued ordinances that prohibited personal service and replaced it with a tribute. The cabildos and encomenderos resisted them, and their enforcement was partial.

hechos/despoblacion-indigena-de-america/.texto: Decline of the Indigenous population of the Americas

In the century and a half after 1492, the Indigenous population of the Americas fell catastrophically, with great differences between regions: the Greater Antilles were almost depopulated, and in central Mexico and the Andes the decline was, by estimates, from half to more than 90%. The figures proposed for 1492 range from about 13 million (Rosenblat, 1954) to between 90 and 112 million (Dobyns, 1966), with a consensus figure of about 54 million (Denevan, 1992). Most specialists, such as Noble David Cook, attribute most deaths to epidemics of smallpox, measles and other diseases against which there was no immunity, aggravated by war, forced labor and social disruption. Others, such as Massimo Livi Bacci, give more weight to those social factors.

hechos/publicacion-de-la-brevisima-de-br.texto: Illustrated edition of A Short Account by Theodor de Bry

Theodor de Bry and his sons published in Frankfurt in 1598 a Latin translation of Las Casas’ A Short Account of the Destruction of the Indies with seventeen engravings of massacres and tortures. Those images, reproduced for centuries, added to the propaganda of the Netherlands and England against Philip II and gave visual form to what in the 20th century came to be called the black legend. Current historiography distinguishes the facts documented by Las Casas from their propagandistic use and from the exaggerations of the European editions.

hechos/debate-sobre-la-leyenda-negra/tit.texto: The debate over the Black Legend and the Rose Legend

hechos/debate-sobre-la-leyenda-negra/res.texto: In 1914 Julián Juderías popularized the expression “black legend” for the hostile image of Spain formed since the 16th century through Las Casas’ A Short Account, De Bry’s engravings and Dutch and English propaganda. The defense of the Spanish work in America, which its critics call the “rose legend” or “white legend,” had in Argentina Rómulo Carbia (1943) and Ricardo Levene, who argued that the Indies were not colonies (1951). It returned to public debate with María Elvira Roca Barea’s Imperiophobia (2016), which José Luis Villacañas criticized in 2019. In American academia, Lewis Hanke highlighted the Spanish debates over the justice of the conquest, and Benjamin Keen responded between 1969 and 1971 that the exploitation of Indigenous labor was structural. Historians such as Ricardo García Cárcel distinguish propaganda and its exaggerations from documented facts, such as the decline of the Indigenous population and forced labor.

hechos/encomienda-y-yanaconazgo/titulo.texto: The encomienda and yanaconazgo in Paraguay, the Río de la Plata and Tucumán

hechos/encomienda-y-yanaconazgo/resumen.texto: The encomienda assigned to a Spanish resident the tribute or labor of a group of Indigenous people, in exchange for protecting them and instructing them in the faith, without granting ownership of their lands. In Paraguay and the Río de la Plata a distinction was made between yanaconas or originarios, who lived permanently in the house or chacra of the encomendero, and mitayos, who served in rotation from their villages. In Tucumán tribute was paid mainly in personal service, which Alfaro’s Ordinances prohibited in 1612 without managing to abolish it. In the Andes the term yanaconas referred to Indigenous people separated from their communities who served Spaniards permanently in houses, chacras and mines. The Crown decreed the general abolition of encomiendas between 1718 and 1721, but in Paraguay they survived until a royal decree of 1803 ordered their incorporation into the Crown.

hechos/poblacion-de-las-misiones-guarani.texto: Epidemics and population of the Guaraní missions

The Jesuits drew up annual censuses of the thirty towns, whose series were studied by, among others, Ernesto Maeder and Alfredo Bolsi. According to those figures, the towns had about 30,000 inhabitants around 1640, after the bandeiras; they exceeded 140,000 in the early 1730s and fell to about 73,000 around 1740, mainly because of a series of epidemics.

hechos/fundacion-de-san-marcos/titulo.texto: Founding of the University of San Marcos

hechos/fundacion-de-san-marcos/resumen.texto: By royal decree of May 12, 1551, Charles V authorized the Dominicans of Lima to found a studium generale with the privileges of the University of Salamanca. It was the first university of the viceroyalty of Peru.

hechos/llegada-de-los-jesuitas-al-tucuma.texto: Arrival of the Jesuits in Tucumán

On November 26, 1585, the Jesuits Francisco de Angulo and Alonso de Bárzana and Brother Juan de Villegas arrived in Santiago del Estero from Peru, called by the bishop of Tucumán, the Dominican Francisco de Vitoria, namesake of the Salamanca theologian. It was the beginning of the Jesuit presence in present-day Argentine territory.

hechos/hospital-de-san-andres-salta-fund.texto: Founding of the hospital of Salta
In 1586 a building intended as a hospital, under the name San Andrés, was erected in Salta beside the hermitage of San Bernardo. It was one of the first in Tucumán.

hechos/provincia-jesuitica-del-paraguay/.texto: Creation of the Jesuit Province of Paraguay

The superior general of the Society of Jesus, Claudio Acquaviva, created in 1604 the province of Paraguay, which covered Tucumán, the Río de la Plata, Paraguay and Chile. Its first provincial, Diego de Torres Bollo, arrived in 1607. The province was centered in Córdoba and existed until the expulsions of 1767 and 1768.

hechos/fundacion-de-san-ignacio-guazu/ti.texto: Founding of the San Ignacio Guazú reduction

hechos/fundacion-de-san-ignacio-guazu/re.texto: At the request of the cacique Arapysandú and with the support of governor Hernandarias, the Jesuits Marcial de Lorenzana and Francisco de San Martín entered the Paraná region in December 1609. In 1610 they began forming the San Ignacio Guazú reduction, the first of the Jesuit Guaraní missions.

hechos/fundacion-de-la-universidad-de-co.texto: Founding of the University of Córdoba

Building on the Colegio Máximo that the Jesuits opened in Córdoba in 1610, Bishop Hernando de Trejo y Sanabria committed on June 19, 1613 to donate his property so that higher studies could be offered, a date the university takes as its founding. A brief from Pope Gregory XV of 1621 and a royal decree of Philip IV of 1622 authorized it to confer degrees. It is the oldest university in present-day Argentine territory.

hechos/fundacion-de-la-universidad-de-ch.texto: Founding of the University of Chuquisaca
Universidad de San Francisco Xavier de Chuquisaca

In 1624 the Jesuits founded in La Plata the University of San Francisco Xavier, authorized to confer degrees. Together with the Academia Carolina for legal practice, created in 1776, it trained the lawyers of Charcas and the Río de la Plata, among them several leaders of 1809 and 1810.

hechos/martirio-de-roque-gonzalez/titulo.texto: Death of Roque González de Santa Cruz at Caaró

hechos/martirio-de-roque-gonzalez/lugar.texto: Caaró, present-day Rio Grande do Sul

hechos/martirio-de-roque-gonzalez/resume.texto: On November 15, 1628, the Jesuits Roque González de Santa Cruz and Alonso Rodríguez were killed at the reduction of Caaró, and two days later Juan del Castillo was killed in another reduction, by Guaraníes led by the cacique Ñezú, who opposed the missions. The Catholic Church canonized them in 1988.

hechos/exodo-del-guaira/lugar.texto: From Guairá to the middle Paraná

hechos/exodo-del-guaira/resumen.texto: Facing attacks by the São Paulo bandeiras, which had destroyed several reductions and captured thousands of Guaraníes to sell them as slaves, Antonio Ruiz de Montoya led the inhabitants of San Ignacio and Loreto down the Paraná, beyond the Guairá falls, to the region of present-day Misiones. Jesuit chronicles speak of some twelve thousand people when they set out, many of whom died on the journey.

hechos/batalla-de-mborore/resumen.texto: On March 11, 1641, on the Uruguay River, the Guaraníes of the reductions, armed with firearms whose use the Jesuits had arranged and led by their caciques, defeated a large São Paulo bandeira. The victory halted slave-raiding incursions into the missions for decades.

hechos/fundacion-del-colegio-de-monserra.texto: Founding of the Colegio de Monserrat

On August 1, 1687, the Córdoba-born priest Ignacio Duarte y Quirós donated his property to the Jesuits to found a boarding college, where students would live and be educated under their direction. After the expulsion of 1767 it passed to the Franciscans.

hechos/imprenta-de-las-misiones/titulo.texto: Printing press of the Guaraní missions

hechos/imprenta-de-las-misiones/resumen.texto: Around 1700 the Jesuits Juan Bautista Neumann and José Serrano set up in the reductions a press with type cast there, and began printing religious books in Guaraní and Spanish in the towns of Loreto, San Javier and Santa María la Mayor. It was the first printing press in the Plata basin, and its best-known work is the translation of Nieremberg’s On the Difference between the Temporal and the Eternal (1705).

hechos/guerra-guaranitica/lugar.texto: San Miguel Arcángel (São Miguel das Missões)

hechos/guerra-guaranitica/resumen.texto: The Guaraníes of the seven towns east of the Uruguay River refused to abandon them, as the Treaty of Madrid of 1750 required, and resisted the boundary commissions and the armies of Spain and Portugal. After a failed campaign in 1754, the allied forces defeated them in 1756 and occupied the towns. The Jesuits’ enemies in Europe accused them of having led the rebellion, an accusation the order denied and which weighed on their expulsion from Portugal (1759) and from Spain (1767). Current historiography views it chiefly as resistance by the Guaraníes themselves.

hechos/batalla-de-caibate/lugar.texto: Caibaté, present-day Rio Grande do Sul

hechos/batalla-de-caibate/resumen.texto: On February 10, 1756, three days after the death of Sepé Tiarayú, the Spanish-Portuguese army, of about 2,500 men, surrounded the Guaraní forces of Nicolás Ñeenguirú (or Ñanguirú) on the hill of Caibaté. According to the victors’ reports, 1,511 Guaraníes died and 154 were taken prisoner, against 4 dead on the allied side.

hechos/hospital-san-roque-legado/titulo.texto: The Bethlehemites and the San Roque hospital of Córdoba

hechos/hospital-san-roque-legado/resumen.texto: In 1762 the Bethlehemite friars began caring for poor patients beside the church of San Roque in Córdoba. Bishop Diego de Salguero y Cabrera, born in the city, bequeathed his property on October 5, 1763 to found a hospital there, and died in 1769. The San Roque hospital opened on October 20, 1800, with the Bethlehemite José de la Asunción as its first director.

hechos/imprenta-de-cordoba/titulo.texto: Printing press of the Jesuits of Córdoba

hechos/imprenta-de-cordoba/resumen.texto: In the mid-1760s the Jesuits of Córdoba installed a printing press in the Colegio de Monserrat, which managed to print few texts before the expulsion of 1767. Years later viceroy Vértiz took it to Buenos Aires, where in 1780 it gave rise to the Real Imprenta de Niños Expósitos.

hechos/expulsion-de-los-jesuitas/titulo.texto: Expulsion of the Jesuits from the Río de la Plata

hechos/expulsion-de-los-jesuitas/resumen.texto: Pursuant to Charles III's pragmatic sanction, Governor Francisco de Paula Bucareli had the Jesuits of Buenos Aires, Córdoba and the other cities arrested in July 1767, and in 1768 those of the thirty Guaraní missions. They passed to civil administrators and other religious orders. In Cuyo, which depended on the governorship of Chile, Governor Antonio de Guill y Gonzaga received the order on August 7 and carried it out at the end of that month in the colleges of Mendoza, San Juan and San Luis, of the Jesuit province of Chile. The order's property, such as the estancias of Córdoba, was placed in the charge of the Junta de Temporalidades and sold, and the population of the missions declined in the following decades.

hechos/expedicion-de-ortiz-de-zarate/tit.texto: Expedition of Ortiz de Zárate and Ciudad Zaratina

hechos/expedicion-de-ortiz-de-zarate/res.texto: The adelantado Juan Ortiz de Zárate sailed from Sanlúcar in October 1572, and in November 1573 reached San Gabriel Island, opposite Colonia, where he built a fort. According to Martín del Barco Centenera, who was in the fleet and recounts it in La Argentina (1602), Ortiz de Zárate captured Abayubá, nephew of the Charrúa cacique Zapicán, and returned him in exchange for a canoe and a Christian. The Charrúa swore revenge, killed about a hundred men, and the Spaniards withdrew to San Gabriel Island and to Martín García, until Juan de Garay, summoned from Santa Fe, defeated the Charrúa in May 1574 at San Salvador. That month the Ciudad Zaratina del San Salvador was founded, and it was abandoned in 1577.

hechos/promulgacion-de-la-recopilacion-d.texto: Promulgation of the Recopilación de las leyes de Indias

Charles II approved in Madrid, by pragmatic sanction of May 18, 1680, the Recopilación de las leyes de los reinos de las Indias, which arranged in nine books the laws scattered since the sixteenth century. Once printed, a royal decree (real cédula) of November 1, 1681 ordered it to be observed. It was the general legal code of the Indies, and in the Río de la Plata it remained in force in practice for the rest of the colonial period, alongside later royal decrees.

hechos/tratado-provisional-de-lisboa-de-.texto: On May 7, 1681, Spain and Portugal signed in Lisbon, after Garro's seizure of the Colonia del Sacramento, a provisional treaty that provided for returning the stronghold to Portugal with its artillery, disapproved of the actions of the Spanish governor, and left the question of sovereignty to a joint commission and, failing agreement, to Pope Innocent XI. Spain ratified it on May 25 and Portugal on June 13. There was no agreement, and the stronghold was handed over to the Portuguese on February 12, 1683.

hechos/motin-de-esquilache/resumen.texto: Beginning on March 23, 1766, a crowd rose up in Madrid against the minister Esquilache, over the scarcity of bread and an edict banning the long cape and the chambergo hat. Charles III lowered prices and dismissed the minister. The secret inquiry that followed, led by Aranda and Campomanes, was one of the antecedents of his 1767 expulsion of the Jesuits from the Spanish dominions, the Río de la Plata included. Teófanes Egido calls it a “motín de corte” (court riot): there were signs of preparation, such as pasquinades and a document of “statutes” dated March 12. The inquiry blamed the Jesuits and the ensenadistas (supporters of Ensenada) without proving it.

hechos/supresion-de-la-compania-de-jesus.texto: Suppression of the Society of Jesus

On July 21, 1773, Pope Clement XIV suppressed the Society of Jesus in almost the whole world with the brief Dominus ac Redemptor, after its expulsions from Portugal (1759), France (1764) and the Spanish dominions (1767). Spanish ambassador José Moñino pressed the pope, and Charles III rewarded him with the title of Count of Floridablanca. The order continued to function in Russia and Prussia, and Pius VII restored it in 1814. In the Río de la Plata the Jesuits had already been expelled in 1767–1768, and the Guaraní missions and estancias were in the hands of civil administrators and other orders.

hechos/entrada-de-diego-de-almagro/resum.texto: Diego de Almagro's expedition to Chile left Cusco in 1535 and was the first European entry into present-day northwestern Argentina: it passed through Tupiza, the old Chicoana, in the Calchaquí valleys, where it stayed two months, and El Shincal, near Londres (Catamarca), and crossed the Andes in the autumn of 1536. The route follows that of Fernández de Oviedo. About the pass, Diego Barros Arana (1884) says it was the San Francisco pass; Rodolfo Raffino (1995) and Christian Vitry (2007) point to Come-Caballos or Pircas Negras.

hechos/tratado-de-lisboa-de-1701/resumen.texto: On June 18, 1701, Spain and Portugal signed in Lisbon an alliance treaty on the eve of the War of the Spanish Succession. Peter II of Portugal backed Philip V, and Spain ceded the Colonia del Sacramento to Portugal, thereby revoking the 1681 agreement. Portugal withdrew its support for Philip V in 1703.

lugares/santiago-del-estero/resumen.texto: The oldest of the cities still standing in present-day Argentine territory. It grew out of El Barco, founded by Juan Núñez de Prado in 1550 and moved several times, and Francisco de Aguirre gave it its name and site in 1553. It was the first seat of the governorship and the bishopric of Tucumán.

lugares/mendoza/resumen.texto: Founded in 1561 by Pedro del Castillo, sent from Chile, in Huarpe territory. Cuyo depended on the governorship of Chile until 1776; its wine and aguardiente were sold in Tucumán and the Río de la Plata.

lugares/san-juan-argentina/resumen.texto: Founded by Juan Jufré in 1562 as San Juan de la Frontera, in Cuyo, in Huarpe territory. It depended on the governorship of Chile until the creation of the Viceroyalty of the Río de la Plata.

lugares/san-miguel-de-tucuman/resumen.texto: Founded by Diego de Villarroel in 1565 at the site of Ibatín and moved in 1685 to its present location. In 1816 it was the seat of the congress that declared independence.

lugares/cordoba-argentina/resumen.texto: Founded by Jerónimo Luis de Cabrera in 1573 as Córdoba de la Nueva Andalucía. It was the seat of the Jesuit Province of Paraguay and of the first university in present-day Argentine territory, and between 1622 and 1695 it had the dry customs house that taxed trade between the Río de la Plata and Tucumán.

lugares/santa-fe-argentina/resumen.texto: Founded by Juan de Garay in 1573 beside the San Javier River and moved between 1651 and 1660 to its present site because of floods and Indigenous attacks. Between 1739 and 1780 it was a required port: vessels coming down from Paraguay had to unload and pay their duties there.

lugares/salta/resumen.texto: Founded by Hernando de Lerma in 1582 in the Lerma valley, on the road from Tucumán to Upper Peru. In the 18th century it was the center of the trade in mules raised in the Litoral and sold for the mines of Potosí.

lugares/corrientes/resumen.texto: Founded in 1588 by Juan Torres de Vera y Aragón as San Juan de Vera de las Siete Corrientes, near the confluence of the Paraná and the Paraguay, to secure the river route between Asunción and Buenos Aires.

lugares/la-rioja-argentina/resumen.texto: Founded in 1591 by the governor of Tucumán Juan Ramírez de Velasco as Todos los Santos de la Nueva Rioja, in Diaguita territory.

lugares/san-salvador-de-jujuy/resumen.texto: Founded by Francisco de Argañaraz in 1593, after two earlier settlements destroyed by the peoples of the region. It was the last city of Tucumán on the road to Upper Peru, and from 1695 it had the dry customs house.

lugares/san-luis-argentina/resumen.texto: City of Cuyo on the road between Mendoza and Córdoba. The founding act was lost: tradition attributes the founding to Luis Jufré de Loaysa y Meneses in 1594, and the city was later moved and refounded.

lugares/catamarca/nombre.texto: San Fernando del Valle de Catamarca

lugares/catamarca/resumen.texto: Founded in 1683 by governor Fernando de Mendoza Mate de Luna, after several failed Spanish settlements in the region, among them Londres.

lugares/londres-catamarca/resumen.texto: Founded in 1558 by Juan Pérez de Zurita and named in honor of Philip II’s marriage to Mary Tudor. It was abandoned and refounded several times during the Calchaquí wars.

lugares/esteco/resumen.texto: City of Tucumán, in present-day southeastern Salta, founded in 1567 as Nuestra Señora de Talavera and merged in 1609 with Madrid de las Juntas. An earthquake razed it on September 13, 1692; the Salta devotion to the Señor and the Virgen del Milagro commemorates that quake.

lugares/concepcion-del-bermejo/resumen.texto: City founded in 1585 by Alonso de Vera y Aragón in the Chaco, on the Bermejo River, to link Tucumán with Paraguay. It was abandoned in 1632 because of attacks by Chaco peoples.

lugares/ibatin/resumen.texto: First site of San Miguel de Tucumán, founded there by Diego de Villarroel in 1565 at the foot of the Quebrada del Portugués. The city moved to its present location in 1685.

lugares/santa-fe-la-vieja/resumen.texto: Ruins of the first Santa Fe, founded by Garay in 1573 and abandoned when the city moved between 1651 and 1660, beside the present town of Cayastá. The excavations begun by Agustín Zapata Gollán in 1949 uncovered the foundations of its churches and houses.

lugares/ruinas-de-sancti-spiritus/resume.texto: Remains of the fort that Sebastián Caboto built in 1527 at the mouth of the Carcarañá, the first Spanish settlement in present-day Argentine territory. An Indigenous attack destroyed it in 1529, and excavations at Puerto Gaboto uncovered its remains.

lugares/puerto-san-julian/resumen.texto: Bay on the Patagonian coast where Magellan’s expedition wintered in 1520 and executed the leaders of a mutiny. There the Europeans had their first contacts with the Tehuelches, whom, according to Pigafetta, Magellan called patagones. In 1578 Francis Drake executed Thomas Doughty at the same place.

lugares/colonia-del-sacramento/resumen.texto: Founded by the Portuguese Manuel Lobo in 1680 across from Buenos Aires. It passed several times between Portuguese and Spanish hands until 1777, and it was the main center of Portuguese and British smuggling on the Río de la Plata; its historic quarter is a World Heritage Site.

lugares/potosi/resumen.texto: Mining city founded at the foot of the Cerro Rico, whose silver was discovered in 1545, and one of the most populous in the Americas at the beginning of the 17th century. Its silver, extracted through the forced labor of the mita, was exported through Lima and also through Buenos Aires, legally or by smuggling.

lugares/casa-de-la-moneda-de-potosi/nomb.texto: Casa de la Moneda de Potosí

lugares/casa-de-la-moneda-de-potosi/resu.texto: Mint founded in 1572 to coin the silver of the Cerro Rico; the present building was built between 1759 and 1773. The pesos of Potosí were the common currency of the Río de la Plata.

lugares/chuquisaca/resumen.texto: City founded around 1538 under the name La Plata, also called Chuquisaca or Charcas, and today Sucre. From 1561 it was the seat of the Audiencia of Charcas, whose district included Tucumán and the Río de la Plata, and from 1624 it also had a university.

lugares/lima/resumen.texto: Founded by Francisco Pizarro in 1535 as Ciudad de los Reyes. It was the capital of the Viceroyalty of Peru, on which the Río de la Plata and Tucumán depended until 1776, and it was the seat of an audiencia, of the Inquisition from 1570, and of the University of San Marcos.

lugares/universidad-de-san-marcos/resume.texto: Created by royal decree of Charles V of May 12, 1551 in Lima, at the request of the Dominicans. It is one of the oldest universities in the Americas and trained a large part of the lettered class of the Viceroyalty of Peru.

lugares/universidad-de-chuquisaca/nombre.texto: Universidad de San Francisco Xavier de Chuquisaca

lugares/universidad-de-chuquisaca/resume.texto: University founded by the Jesuits in 1624 in La Plata (Chuquisaca). There, law was studied above all at the Academia Carolina created in 1776, by Mariano Moreno, Juan José Castelli and Bernardo de Monteagudo, among other protagonists of 1809 and 1810.

lugares/colegio-de-monserrat/resumen.texto: Royal Convictorio College of Our Lady of Montserrat, founded in Córdoba on August 1, 1687 with the property of Ignacio Duarte y Quirós and run by the Jesuits until 1767. In the 1760s one of the first printing presses in present-day Argentine territory operated there; today it depends on the National University of Córdoba.

lugares/estancias-jesuiticas-de-cordoba/.texto: Jesuit Block and Estancias of Córdoba

Ensemble made up of the Jesuit Block of Córdoba (church, college and university) and five rural estancias (Caroya, Jesús María, Santa Catalina, Alta Gracia and La Candelaria), founded between 1616 and 1683 to sustain the colleges, with the labor of African slaves and Indigenous people. It has been a World Heritage Site since 2000.

lugares/manzana-de-las-luces/resumen.texto: Block in central Buenos Aires where the Jesuits opened the Colegio de San Ignacio in 1661 and built the church of San Ignacio, the oldest surviving church in the city. After the expulsion, the Real Colegio de San Carlos operated there and, from 1821, the University of Buenos Aires.

lugares/hospital-de-san-andres-salta/res.texto: Hospital built in 1586 next to the hermitage of San Bernardo, in Salta, one of the first in Tucumán. It closed and reopened several times; in 1805 it was run by the Bethlemites, and since 1846 the building has been the convent of San Bernardo of the Carmelites.

lugares/hospital-san-roque-cordoba/resum.texto: Hospital in Córdoba, next to the church of San Roque, where the Bethlemites cared for poor patients from 1762. It was built with the bequest of Bishop Diego de Salguero y Cabrera (1763) and opened in 1800; from 1878 it was the teaching hospital of the Faculty of Medicine of Córdoba.

lugares/san-ignacio-mini/resumen.texto: Guaraní Jesuit reduction founded around 1610 in Guairá, moved in 1632 because of attacks by the bandeirantes and established at its present site in Misiones at the end of the 17th century. Its ruins of red sandstone, with Baroque decoration made by Guaraní craftsmen, have been a World Heritage Site since 1984.

lugares/loreto-misiones/resumen.texto: Guaraní reduction founded in Guairá and moved to the present territory of Misiones during the exodus of 1631 and 1632. At the beginning of the 18th century it was one of the towns where books were printed in Guaraní.

lugares/yapeyu/resumen.texto: Guaraní reduction founded in 1627 on the banks of the Uruguay River, with the participation of Roque González de Santa Cruz, and the southernmost of the missions, with large cattle estancias. José de San Martín was born there.

lugares/santa-ana-misiones/resumen.texto: Guaraní reduction founded in Tape and moved to the bank of the Paraná, in present-day Misiones, during the attacks of the bandeirantes in the 1630s. Its ruins are part of the group of Guaraní Jesuit missions declared a World Heritage Site in 1983 and 1984.

lugares/santisima-trinidad-de-parana/res.texto: Guaraní Jesuit reduction founded in 1706 in present-day Paraguay, the last of the thirty. Its ruins, with a large stone church and sculpted friezes, have been a World Heritage Site since 1993.

lugares/jesus-de-tavarangue/resumen.texto: Guaraní Jesuit reduction founded in 1685 and moved several times; its large church was left unfinished when the expulsion of 1767 took place. It has been a World Heritage Site since 1993.

lugares/sao-miguel-das-missoes/nombre.texto: San Miguel Arcángel (São Miguel das Missões)

lugares/sao-miguel-das-missoes/resumen.texto: Reduction of San Miguel, one of the seven towns east of the Uruguay River that the Treaty of Madrid of 1750 handed over to Portugal. It was the center of Guaraní resistance in 1754-1756; its ruins, in present-day Rio Grande do Sul, are a World Heritage Site.
